stem: Under Virginia's current distracted-driving law, what is a driver prohibited from doing with a handheld personal communications device while driving on a highway?

options.text: Holding it at all
options.rationale: Correct. The statute prohibits holding the device, not merely typing on it.

options.text: Reading or sending text messages, but holding it is allowed
options.rationale: This was the older, narrower rule. The law was broadened to cover holding the device at all.

options.text: Using it for anything other than navigation
options.rationale: There is no navigation carve-out for holding the device; hands-free use is what the law permits.

options.text: Using it only while the vehicle is in motion above 25 mph
options.rationale: No speed threshold appears in the statute.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-818.2 makes it unlawful to hold a handheld personal communications device while driving on a highway. A first offense is $125 and a second or subsequent offense is $250, with a mandatory $250 fine in a highway work zone. Anything that reduces this to a 'texting ban' understates it.

accuracy.note: Enacted 2020 cc. 250, 543; work-zone fine added 2023 cc. 557, 558.

stem: In Virginia, drivers under 18 are subject to a separate, stricter cell phone ban than adult drivers.

options.text: True
options.rationale: This described the law before 2021, when § 46.2-1078.1 imposed a total ban on drivers under 18.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct. That section was repealed and the handheld rule is now uniform across ages.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-1078.1, the under-18 total cell phone ban, was repealed effective January 1, 2021 by the same act that created the general handheld prohibition. The rule in § 46.2-818.2 now applies uniformly to every driver and is a primary offense for everyone — an officer may stop a vehicle for it alone.

stem: You are on a four-lane highway with two lanes in your direction. Which stopped vehicle triggers Virginia's Move Over duty?

options.text: Only police, fire, and rescue vehicles with flashing lights
options.rationale: This was the pre-2023 scope. The duty has since been extended.

options.text: Only emergency vehicles and tow trucks
options.rationale: Still too narrow — the 2023 amendment reached ordinary vehicles.

options.text: Any stationary vehicle with hazard flashers on, caution signs displayed, or lit flares
options.rationale: Correct. Subsection B covers ordinary vehicles showing any of these.

options.text: Any vehicle stopped on the shoulder for any reason
options.rationale: Close, but the statute lists specific signals — flashers, caution signs, or lit flares — not merely being stopped.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-861.1(B), added effective July 1, 2023, extends the Move Over duty beyond emergency vehicles to any stationary vehicle with hazard warning flashers activated, caution signs displayed, or lit flares or torches. Change lanes away when you can; when that is unreasonable or unsafe, proceed with due caution at a safe speed.

accuracy.note: Amended by 2023 cc. 616, 617. The former Move Over section, § 46.2-921.1, was repealed by Acts 2019 c. 850 — citations to it are dead.

stem: A driver fails to move over or slow down for a stopped vehicle displaying flashing blue and red emergency lights. How is that violation classified in Virginia?

options.text: Reckless driving
options.rationale: Correct. Violating the emergency-vehicle branch of the statute is reckless driving.

options.text: A traffic infraction
options.rationale: That is the classification for the ordinary-vehicle branch added in 2023, not the emergency-vehicle branch.

options.text: A Class 1 misdemeanor
options.rationale: The statute does not classify it this way.

options.text: A civil penalty with no points
options.rationale: Reckless driving carries six demerit points; this is not a civil penalty.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-861.1(A) makes failure to move over for a vehicle displaying flashing blue, red, or amber emergency lights reckless driving. The 2023 subsection (B), covering ordinary vehicles with hazard flashers, caution signs, or flares, is a traffic infraction instead. Subsection C adds suspension up to one year for property damage and up to two years for injury or death.

stem: Under Virginia's Zero Tolerance law, what blood alcohol concentration range applies to a driver under 21?

options.text: 0.01% to under 0.08%
options.rationale: The threshold is 0.02%, not 0.01%.

options.text: 0.02% to under 0.08%
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: 0.02% to under 0.05%
options.rationale: The upper bound is 0.08%, where the general DUI offense takes over.

options.text: Any detectable amount of alcohol
options.rationale: 'Zero tolerance' names the policy, but the statute sets a measurable 0.02% floor.

explanation: Va. Code § 18.2-266.1 applies to drivers under 21 with a BAC of 0.02% or more but less than 0.08%. It is a Class 1 misdemeanor carrying a one-year license suspension and a minimum $500 fine or 50 hours of community service. At 0.08% or more, the general DUI statute § 18.2-266 applies at any age.

accuracy.note: Rule stable 2021-2026; amended 2026 c. 1112 without changing the BAC range.

stem: At what blood alcohol concentration is a Virginia driver guilty of DUI regardless of observed impairment?

options.text: More than 0.08%
options.rationale: A common misstatement. Exactly 0.08% is already an offense — the statute says 'or more'.

options.text: 0.08% or more
options.rationale: Correct, and the precise wording matters.

options.text: 0.10% or more
options.rationale: Virginia lowered its per se limit to 0.08% in 2005.

options.text: 0.05% or more
options.rationale: 0.05% is a level at which effects are measurable, not the per se limit.

explanation: Va. Code § 18.2-266 sets the per se limit at 0.08 grams or more per 210 liters of breath (or per 100 milliliters of blood). Course material that says a driver must 'exceed' 0.08 is wrong at exactly 0.08 — the safe formulation is always '0.08 or more'.

stem: A driver arrested for DUI refuses a breath test for the first time. What follows under Virginia's Implied Consent law?

options.text: A civil offense with a one-year license suspension
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A Class 1 misdemeanor with a three-year revocation
options.rationale: That is a second or subsequent refusal within 10 years.

options.text: No consequence, since testing is voluntary
options.rationale: Operating on a Virginia highway is itself consent to testing after a DUI arrest.

options.text: A 90-day suspension and a mandatory driver improvement clinic
options.rationale: That combination belongs to demerit-point accumulation, not to test refusal.

explanation: Va. Code § 18.2-268.2 makes operating a vehicle on a Virginia highway consent to breath or blood testing if arrested for DUI. Under § 18.2-268.3 a first refusal is a civil offense with a one-year suspension; a second or subsequent refusal within 10 years is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a three-year revocation.

stem: Who commits an offense when marijuana is consumed in a moving vehicle on a Virginia public highway?

options.text: The driver only
options.rationale: The statute reaches passengers as well.

options.text: The driver and any passenger who consumes
options.rationale: Correct — § 4.1-1107 applies to both.

options.text: Nobody, since possession by adults is lawful
options.rationale: Lawful possession is not lawful consumption in a moving vehicle.

options.text: Only a driver under 21
options.rationale: The prohibition is not age-limited.

explanation: Va. Code § 4.1-1107 makes it a Class 4 misdemeanor for the driver or any passenger to use or consume marijuana in a moving vehicle on a public highway. An 'open container' is any vessel other than the original sealed manufacturer's container. Note also that Virginia has no per se THC blood limit — § 18.2-266's per se list covers cocaine, methamphetamine, PCP, and MDMA only, so marijuana impairment must be proved as impairment.

stem: Regardless of the posted speed limit, driving at what speed is reckless driving in Virginia?

options.text: In excess of 75 mph
options.rationale: Not a threshold in the statute.

options.text: In excess of 80 mph
options.rationale: This was the law until July 1, 2020, and is the most common stale answer on this topic.

options.text: In excess of 85 mph
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: In excess of 90 mph
options.rationale: Higher than the statute requires.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-862 makes it reckless driving to drive 20 mph or more over the posted limit, or in excess of 85 mph regardless of the limit. The absolute threshold was raised from 80 to 85 mph effective July 1, 2020 — any course written before then teaches 80.

accuracy.note: Threshold raised from 80 to 85 mph by 2020 cc. 444, 445.

stem: How old do you have to be before Virginia will issue you a learner's permit?

options.text: 15 years
options.rationale: Six months short.

options.text: 15 years and 6 months
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: 16 years
options.rationale: 16 years and 3 months is the minimum for a license, not a permit.

options.text: 16 years and 3 months
options.rationale: That is the minimum licensing age.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-335 sets the minimum learner's permit age at 15 years and 6 months. The permit must be held nine months, or until age 18, whichever comes first (§ 46.2-335.2), and the minimum age for a driver's license is 16 years and 3 months (§ 46.2-334).

stem: How much supervised practice driving must a Virginia learner's permit holder complete, and how much of it must be after sunset?

options.text: 40 hours, at least 10 after sunset
options.rationale: Both figures are short of Virginia's requirement.

options.text: 45 hours, at least 15 after sunset
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: 45 hours, at least 10 after sunset
options.rationale: The total is right; the night-driving portion is 15 hours.

options.text: 50 hours, at least 15 after sunset
options.rationale: Virginia requires 45 hours, not 50.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-335 requires 45 hours of behind-the-wheel practice, at least 15 of them after sunset, certified by a parent, foster parent, or legal guardian.

stem: During the first year holding a Virginia provisional license, how many passengers under 21 may the driver carry?

options.text: None
options.rationale: One is permitted, and family and household members are exempt entirely.

options.text: One
options.rationale: Correct, not counting family or household members.

options.text: Three
options.rationale: Three becomes available after the first year, and only in specific circumstances.

options.text: No limit, as long as everyone is belted
options.rationale: The passenger restriction is independent of the belt requirement.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-334.01 limits a provisional licensee to one passenger under 21 during the first year. After the first year the limit rises to three, and only when driving to or from a school-sponsored activity, when accompanied by a licensed driver 21 or older, or in an emergency. Family and household members are exempt from both limits. Enforcement is secondary — an officer may not stop a vehicle for this alone.

stem: In Virginia, an adult riding in the back seat is not required to wear a safety belt.

options.text: True
options.rationale: This was the law until July 1, 2025, when the requirement was extended to every seat.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct — every occupant 18 and older must be belted in every seat.

explanation: The Christopher King Law, amending Va. Code § 46.2-1094 effective July 1, 2025, requires every occupant 18 and older to wear a safety belt in every seat, including the back, whenever the vehicle is in motion on a public highway. It also covers rideshare drivers and passengers. Note that enforcement remains secondary — the statute still bars stopping a vehicle for this alone — and the civil penalty is $25 with no demerit points.

accuracy.note: Amended by 2025 c. 414 (HB 2475). Virginia did NOT move to primary enforcement.

stem: Until what point must a child ride in a rear-facing child restraint in Virginia?

options.text: Until age 1, or 20 pounds
options.rationale: An older national guideline, not Virginia's current rule.

options.text: Until at least age 2, or the manufacturer's minimum forward-facing weight limit
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Until age 4
options.rationale: Longer than the statute requires for rear-facing.

options.text: Until the child weighs 40 pounds
options.rationale: Virginia's rule is age-based with a manufacturer-limit alternative, not a flat weight.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-1095 requires rear-facing until the child reaches at least age 2 or the minimum weight limit for a forward-facing seat set by the manufacturer. A child restraint device is required through age 7 — that is, until the eighth birthday — and children 8 to under 18 must use a safety belt. Restraints go in the rear seat unless the vehicle has no passenger airbag or it is disabled.

stem: Under what circumstances may a person under 16 ride in the open cargo bed of a pickup truck on a Virginia highway?

options.text: Never, without exception
options.rationale: Two narrow exceptions exist.

options.text: In an authorized parade, or in farm operations moving between fields
options.rationale: Correct — these are the statute's only exceptions.

options.text: When traveling under 25 mph on a rural road
options.rationale: No speed or road-type exception exists.

options.text: When being transported to or from a hunting trip
options.rationale: Hunting is specifically not an exception.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-1156.1 prohibits transporting anyone under 16 in the rear cargo area of a pickup on a Virginia highway, with exceptions only for authorized parades and for farm operations moving between fields.

accuracy.note: The prohibition and exceptions are confirmed; the section does not state a penalty amount.

stem: For a Virginia auto policy effective in 2026, what are the minimum liability limits?

options.rationale: The pre-2022 minimums.
These applied to policies effective from 2022 through the end of 2024.
Correct for policies effective on or after January 1, 2025.
Higher than Virginia requires; these are common optional limits.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-472 phased in higher minimums in two steps: $30,000/$60,000/$20,000 for policies effective January 1, 2022 through December 31, 2024, then $50,000/$100,000/$25,000 for policies effective on or after January 1, 2025. The figures are bodily injury for one person, bodily injury for two or more, and property damage.

accuracy.note: Two-step phase-in enacted by 2021 Sp. Sess. I c. 273.

stem: A Virginia vehicle owner may pay an uninsured motor vehicle fee to DMV instead of carrying liability insurance.

options.text: True
options.rationale: This was possible until July 1, 2024, at a cost of $500 — and it never provided the motorist any coverage.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct. The fee was eliminated and insurance is now mandatory.

explanation: The uninsured motor vehicle fee was eliminated effective July 1, 2024 by 2023 SB 951. Every vehicle registered in Virginia must now carry liability insurance meeting the statutory minimums, or else a bond, cash deposit, or self-insurance certificate. Driving or registering uninsured means suspension, a $600 noncompliance fee, and an SR-22 filing for three years.

authority.cite: Virginia DMV, new laws effective July 1, 2024

accuracy.note: The DMV insurance-requirements page still carries a stale reference to a payment plan for 'the statutory fee'. The statute controls.

stem: If your insurer decides not to renew your auto policy, how far in advance must it notify you?

options.text: 10 days
options.rationale: Too short; this figure appears in some course material and is wrong.

options.text: 30 days
options.rationale: A common answer, and what this course teaches — but the statute requires 45.

options.text: 45 days
options.rationale: Correct under § 38.2-2212(E).

options.text: 60 days
options.rationale: Longer than the statute requires.

divergence: The course grades 30 days as correct. Virginia law requires 45 days' notice of cancellation or nonrenewal, or 15 days where the ground is non-payment of premium.
explanation: Va. Code § 38.2-2212(E) requires 45 days' notice of cancellation or nonrenewal, or 15 days where the ground is non-payment of premium.

stem: Virginia's aggressive driving statute lists specific predicate offenses. Which of these is NOT among them?

options.text: Failing to yield the right-of-way
options.rationale: This IS listed in § 46.2-868.1 — and the course keys it as the exception, which is backwards.

options.text: Following too closely
options.rationale: Listed in the statute.

options.text: Accelerating rapidly into traffic
options.rationale: Correct — this phrasing does not appear among the statute's predicate offenses.

options.text: Passing on the right off the roadway
options.rationale: Listed in the statute.

divergence: The course grades 'failing to yield right-of-way' as the exception, but § 46.2-868.1 lists failure to stop or yield the right-of-way among its predicate offenses — and the course's own reading page says so.
explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-868.1 defines aggressive driving in two parts: the driver commits one or more listed violations, and either is a hazard to another person or commits the violation intending to harass, intimidate, injure, or obstruct. Being a hazard is enough on its own; intent is what raises the charge from a Class 2 to a Class 1 misdemeanor. Failure to stop or yield the right-of-way is on the list. The course's own pages disagree with each other on whether intent is required; the statute settles it.

stem: What occupancy qualifies a vehicle for toll-free HOV travel on I-66 inside the Capital Beltway during restricted hours?

options.text: Two or more occupants
options.rationale: This was the rule until December 5, 2022, when the requirement rose to three.

options.text: Three or more occupants
options.rationale: Correct, with an E-ZPass Flex switched to HOV mode.

options.text: Four or more occupants
options.rationale: Higher than any Virginia express facility requires.

options.text: Any occupancy, as long as you have an E-ZPass
options.rationale: A standard E-ZPass pays the dynamic toll; occupancy is what makes travel free.

explanation: I-66 inside the Beltway changed from HOV-2 to HOV-3+ on December 5, 2022. Restrictions and tolling apply eastbound 5:30–9:30 a.m. and westbound 3–7 p.m., Monday through Friday excluding federal holidays — not around the clock. I-66 outside the Beltway, the I-495 Express Lanes, and the I-95/I-395 Express Lanes are all HOV-3+ as well.

stem: A carpool of three people with a standard E-ZPass travels free on the Northern Virginia express lanes.

options.text: True
options.rationale: Occupancy alone is not enough — the transponder must be able to declare HOV mode.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct. Toll-free HOV travel requires an E-ZPass Flex switched to HOV ON.

explanation: An E-ZPass Flex — the transponder with the HOV switch — is required for toll-free HOV travel on the I-66, I-495, and I-95/I-395 express lanes. A standard E-ZPass is charged the dynamic toll even with three or more occupants aboard.

stem: How does an HOV violation in Northern Virginia (Planning District 8) differ from one elsewhere in the Commonwealth?

options.text: It carries escalating fines and demerit points on repeat offenses
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: It is a criminal misdemeanor rather than an infraction
options.rationale: It remains a traffic infraction.

options.text: There is no difference; the penalty is uniform statewide
options.rationale: The statute sets a separate escalating schedule for Planning District 8.

options.text: It results in immediate license suspension
options.rationale: No suspension attaches to an HOV violation.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 33.2-501 an HOV violation is generally a $100 traffic infraction, not a moving violation, with no demerit points. In Planning District 8 the schedule escalates: $125 first, $250 for a second within five years, $500 for a third, $1,000 for a fourth and beyond — and three demerit points attach to each second and subsequent offense within five years. Motorcycles, transit buses, emergency and law-enforcement vehicles, and vehicles with clean special fuel plates are exempt.

stem: When must you NOT stop for a school bus that is loading or unloading with its stop arm out?

options.text: Never — you must always stop, from every direction
options.rationale: Close, but the statute does provide a divided-highway exception.

options.text: When the bus is on the other roadway of a divided highway
options.rationale: Correct — also an access road or a driveway separated by a physical barrier or unpaved area.

options.text: Whenever you are headed the other way, on any kind of road
options.rationale: Opposite-direction traffic must stop unless the roadways are divided.

options.text: When there are two or more lanes in your direction
options.rationale: Lane count alone does not create an exception; separation of the roadways does.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-859 requires stopping for a stopped school bus loading or unloading from any direction, except where the bus is on the other roadway of a divided highway, on an access road, or on a driveway separated by a physical barrier or unpaved area. Violation is reckless driving. Localities may also authorize stop-arm cameras under § 46.2-844, with a $250 civil penalty.

accuracy.note: The course states the exception's scope two incompatible ways and hides it in a hover tooltip. The statute is the authority here.

stem: You receive a mailed citation from a photo speed monitoring device in a Virginia work zone. What is the consequence?

options.text: A civil penalty up to $100, not added to your driving record or used for insurance
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A traffic infraction with three demerit points
options.rationale: A mailed citation is a civil penalty and carries no points.

options.text: A civil penalty up to $500 plus points
options.rationale: The cap is $100 and no points attach.

options.text: Nothing enforceable, since camera citations are advisory
options.rationale: They are enforceable civil penalties against the vehicle.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-882.1 authorizes photo speed monitoring where a vehicle exceeds the limit by at least 10 mph, with a civil penalty not exceeding $100. A mailed citation 'shall not be made part of the operating record' and cannot be used for insurance purposes. If an officer instead issues a summons in person at the time, that conviction does go on the record. The 2026 session limited work-zone cameras to when workers are actually present.

accuracy.note: 2026 chapters 963-970, 986, 1033 overhauled the program. Some provisions have delayed effective dates not yet identified — avoid dated questions on camera enforcement.

stem: An adult driver accumulates 12 demerit points in 12 months. What does DMV require?

options.text: An advisory letter only
options.rationale: That is the response at 8 points in 12 months.

options.text: A mandatory driver improvement clinic
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A 90-day license suspension
options.rationale: Suspension attaches at 18 points in 12 months (or 24 in 24).

options.text: License revocation for one year
options.rationale: Revocation for a year applies to a third under-18 violation, not to this threshold.

explanation: For drivers 18 and older: 8 points in 12 months (or 12 in 24) brings an advisory letter; 12 in 12 months (or 18 in 24) brings a mandatory driver improvement clinic; 18 in 12 months (or 24 in 24) brings a 90-day suspension plus the clinic. Since July 1, 2026, a driver facing that suspension must be offered a written choice between it and nine months in the Intelligent Speed Assistance Program, with 30 days to respond.

stem: A driver fails to stop for a pedestrian lawfully crossing and causes serious bodily injury. How is that charged in Virginia?

options.text: A traffic infraction only
options.rationale: That is the charge when no serious injury results.

options.text: A Class 1 misdemeanor
options.rationale: Correct, where the victim is a vulnerable road user and the injury is serious or fatal.

options.text: Reckless driving
options.rationale: Not the classification this statute assigns.

options.text: A civil penalty payable to the locality
options.rationale: This is a criminal charge, not a civil penalty.

explanation: 2025 SB 1416 makes failure to stop for a pedestrian a traffic infraction, escalating to a Class 1 misdemeanor when it results in serious bodily injury or the death of a vulnerable road user lawfully crossing a highway.

authority.cite: 2025 Va. Acts, SB 1416; Division of Legislative Services, In Due Course 2025

stem: Put the steps of a safe lane change in order.

steps.text: Check mirrors
steps.why: The mirrors come before anything else because they tell you whether a lane change is available at all, and what is closing from behind.

steps.text: Signal
steps.why: The signal goes out as soon as you intend to move, before the blind-zone check, so following drivers get the longest possible warning.

steps.text: Check the blind zone
steps.why: The head check is last before moving because a mirror-only check misses the lane beside you, and a check done earlier is stale by the time you move.

steps.text: Adjust speed
steps.why: Match the speed of the lane you are entering before you enter it; steering into faster traffic at the wrong speed makes the car behind brake for you.

steps.text: Move when the way is clear
steps.why: The move waits on the gap, not on the signal. A signal is a request; it is not a right of way.

steps.text: Use minimal steering
steps.why: A lane change at speed needs only a slight steering input. A sharp turn of the wheel unsettles the vehicle and can carry it into the lane beyond.

steps.text: Establish lane position
steps.why: Center the vehicle in the new lane before doing anything else. The maneuver is not finished until the car is settled.

steps.text: Cancel the signal
steps.why: A signal left on tells other drivers you are about to move again. Canceling it is the last step of the maneuver, not housekeeping afterwards.

explanation: The VDOE sequence checks mirrors before signaling, and checks the blind zone after signaling — the signal goes out early so other drivers have the most warning, while the blind-zone check happens as late as possible so it reflects current conditions. Canceling the signal is part of the maneuver, not an afterthought.

source.basis: VDOE Module 13, Key Concepts for Lesson 3

authority.cite: VDOE, Curriculum Guide for Behind-the-Wheel In-Car Instruction, Module 13, Key Concepts for Lesson 3

stem: Your right tires drop onto the shoulder at speed. Put the recovery steps in order.

steps.text: Keep both hands firmly on the wheel and hold your lane position on the shoulder
steps.why: The first job is not to react. A firm grip and a straight line along the shoulder prevent the instinctive jerk back toward the pavement, which at speed is what starts a rollover.

steps.text: Ease off the accelerator and let the vehicle slow — do not brake
steps.why: Speed comes down by coasting. Braking with two wheels on gravel and two on asphalt gives the two sides different grip and drags the car sideways.

steps.text: Determine a target and path of travel back onto the pavement
steps.why: Choose where you will come back on, a point where the edge is low and the road ahead is clear, before you steer, so the steering has an aim.

steps.text: With speed under control, turn the wheel toward the target
steps.why: Only once speed is under control: enough steering to aim at the return point, no more. Turning while still fast is how the car ends up across the center line.

steps.text: Ease the vehicle onto the paved surface
steps.why: Climb the edge gently. A gradual return lets the tires take the lip one at a time instead of the whole car lurching back onto the road.

steps.text: Counter-steer as the front tire regains the roadway to hold lane position
steps.why: As the front tire regains pavement it grips suddenly and the car tries to swing toward the center line. A prompt counter-steer straightens it in the lane.

explanation: The instinct to brake and steer back immediately is what turns a shoulder drop into a rollover or a head-on. VDOE's sequence removes speed first without braking, picks the return point before touching the wheel, steers toward it only once speed is under control, eases over the edge rather than lurching, and finishes with a counter-steer, because the tire regaining pavement grips suddenly.

source.basis: VDOE Module 13, Key Concepts for Lesson 6

authority.cite: VDOE, Curriculum Guide for Behind-the-Wheel In-Car Instruction, Module 13, Key Concepts for Lesson 6 (Off Road Recovery, p. 34)

accuracy.note: Keyed to the guide's own bullet order on p. 34: hands firm, ease off the accelerator, do not brake, determine target and path of travel, with speed under control turn toward target, ease onto the paved surface, counter-steer. The guide's 'drop both tires off roadway' bullet is a vehicle state rather than a step and sits between target and steering in a list that is not numbered, so it is not a step here.

stem: Ana is 16 and filling out her learner's permit application. She marks the box saying she wants to be an organ, eye and tissue donor. While she is still under 18, what does that mark actually do?

options.text: Nothing; a donor choice made before age 18 has no legal standing and she must register again as an adult.
options.rationale: The Code lets a minor who is old enough for a permit (15 years and 6 months) record a donor decision herself, so the mark is a real registration, not a placeholder.

options.text: It records her decision, but if she died before turning 18 a parent or guardian could still change or cancel it.
options.rationale: Correct. A permit-age minor may register as a donor, and the law reserves to a parent the power to amend or revoke that gift while the donor is an unemancipated minor.

options.text: It is final and binding; not even her parents could override it.
options.rationale: That is the rule once the donor is an adult. For an unemancipated minor, a reasonably available parent may revoke or amend the gift after the minor's death.

options.text: It is not permitted; only a parent can make the donor decision for anyone under 18.
options.rationale: A parent may make a gift on a minor's behalf, but the statute also lets the minor decide for herself once she is eligible to apply for a license.

explanation: Virginia lets you sign up as an organ, eye and tissue donor on your permit, license or ID application at any age the DMV will accept you, because Va. Code § 32.1-291.4 allows a minor to make an anatomical gift once they are at least 15 years and 6 months old. Until you turn 18, though, your parents keep the last word: under § 32.1-291.8(G) a parent who can be reached may revoke or change the gift if an unemancipated minor dies. The Driver's Manual says the same thing in plain terms, which is why it urges you to tell your family what you decided.

source.basis: course Session 1, page 42 (bank item 1.16); Virginia Driver's Manual Section 7, p. 34

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 7, p. 34 (Organ, Eye and Tissue Donation)

accuracy.note: § 32.1-291.4(1)(b): a minor may make the gift if 'authorized under state law to apply for a driver's license because the donor is at least 15 years and six months of age'. § 32.1-291.8(G): if an unemancipated minor donor dies, a reasonably available parent may revoke or amend the gift. Manual p. 34: under 18 you may check yes, but parents and guardians make the final decision. All three agree.

stem: You are 19 and your Virginia driver's license shows you as a registered donor. If you died in a crash, your family could legally cancel that decision.

options.text: True
options.rationale: That was possible only while you were an unemancipated minor. Once an adult has recorded an anatomical gift, other people are barred from revoking it unless the donor said otherwise.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct. An adult's registered donor decision stands on its own; Va. Code § 32.1-291.8(A) bars anyone else from making, amending or revoking it.

explanation: Virginia's anatomical gift law gives an adult donor's own registration the final say. Va. Code § 32.1-291.8(A) says that when a donor has made a gift, a person other than the donor is barred from making, amending or revoking it, unless the donor left a clear contrary instruction. The parent override in subsection G applies only to unemancipated minors, so it ends at 18. The Driver's Manual puts it simply: at 18 or older, your registered decision will be honored. Telling your family is still worth doing, but it is so they are not surprised, not because they get a vote.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 7, p. 34 (Organ, Eye and Tissue Donation)

accuracy.note: § 32.1-291.8(A): 'in the absence of an express, contrary indication by the donor, a person other than the donor is barred from making, amending, or revoking an anatomical gift' the donor made. Subsection G (parental revocation) is limited to unemancipated minors. Manual p. 34: 'If you are age 18 or older, your registered decision to be a donor will be honored.'

stem: You are studying the Virginia Driver's Manual for the knowledge exam. According to the manual itself, what is its legal status?

options.text: It is the official text of Virginia traffic law and is what courts apply.
options.rationale: The manual says the reverse: it is an informational tool that does not supersede any statute. Courts apply the Code of Virginia, not the manual.

options.text: It is a study guide to the traffic laws; the laws themselves are in the Code of Virginia, Title 46.2, which controls if the two differ.
options.rationale: Correct. The manual describes itself as a general guide that is not a substitute for the Code, and points readers to Title 46.2 for the actual motor vehicle laws.

options.text: It is legally binding only on drivers under 18 who completed driver education.
options.rationale: The manual is not binding on anyone as law. Age has nothing to do with it; the Code of Virginia governs every driver.

options.text: It fills in as law for any situation the Code of Virginia does not cover.
options.rationale: The manual never stands in for a statute. Where the Code is silent, the manual's advice is still just advice.

explanation: The Driver's Manual is the DMV's study guide. Its own introduction says it should be used as a general guide to the motor vehicle laws and not as a substitute for the Code of Virginia, and its back cover repeats that it does not supersede the Code or any other statute, pointing you to Title 46.2 (Motor Vehicles) for the real text. That matters when a number in the manual is out of date, which happens: the law on the books is what a court or DMV will apply. When you need to be sure, read the section at law.lis.virginia.gov.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), introduction (p. 1) and back cover

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), introduction, p. 1, and back cover

accuracy.note: Introduction: the manual 'should be used as a general guide to the motor vehicle laws but not as a substitute for the Code of Virginia'. Back cover: 'This manual is an informational tool. It does not supercede the Code of Virginia, Virginia Administrative Code or any other statute. To view Virginia's motor vehicle laws, refer to the Virginia Code, Title 46.2.' The April 2026 edition itself still prints the pre-2025 liability minimums and the abolished uninsured motor vehicle fee (p. 34), a live example of why the Code controls.

stem: Your family moves from Maryland to Virginia and brings the car you will be driving. Within how many days of the move must that car be titled and registered in Virginia?

options.text: 10 days
options.rationale: No Virginia vehicle deadline is that short. Ten days is a guess below the real figure.

options.text: 30 days
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual and DMV both give new residents 30 days to title and register a vehicle and get Virginia plates.

options.text: 60 days
options.rationale: Sixty days is how long a new resident may keep driving on an out-of-state driver's license (Va. Code § 46.2-308). The car's deadline is shorter.

options.text: 6 months
options.rationale: Six months is the grace period Va. Code § 46.2-656 gives a nonresident visitor who keeps home-state plates. Someone who has moved here is a resident, and that grace period does not apply.

explanation: When you become a Virginia resident, the car and the driver run on different clocks. The vehicle must be titled and registered with Virginia plates within 30 days of the move, according to Section 7 of the Driver's Manual and the DMV's 'New to Virginia' page; Va. Code § 46.2-600 uses the same 30-day window for any Virginia resident who buys or receives a vehicle. The driver gets 60 days to trade an out-of-state license for a Virginia one under § 46.2-308. Before DMV will register the car it must also carry Virginia liability insurance and pass a safety inspection.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 7, p. 33 (Titles, Registrations, License Plates, Decals)

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 7, p. 33 (Titles, Registrations, License Plates, Decals)

accuracy.note: Manual p. 33: title and register and obtain Virginia plates within 30 days of moving to Virginia. DMV page: 'title your vehicle within 30 days of moving to Virginia' and 'register it ... within 30 days of moving here'; driver's license within 60 days. § 46.2-600 states 30 days from purchase or transfer for residents; the mover's 30-day clock is stated by DMV and the manual rather than in the section text, so the DMV page is the primary authority for the mover case. § 46.2-656's six-month allowance is for nonresident owners only. § 46.2-308: sixty days for a newly resident licensed driver.

stem: A car registered in Virginia and driven on public roads has to pass a state safety inspection and carry the windshield sticker. How often is a new inspection required?

options.text: Once, when the car is first titled in Virginia
options.rationale: There is no one-time inspection in Virginia law. The requirement repeats for as long as the vehicle is registered and used on the highway.

options.text: Every 12 months
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-1158 requires reinspection within 12 months of the first inspection and at least once every 12 months after that.

options.text: Every two years
options.rationale: Two years is the cycle for the emissions inspection in Northern Virginia, a separate program run by DEQ. The safety inspection is yearly.

options.text: Only when the car is sold to a new owner
options.rationale: The inspection follows the calendar, not the title. A change of owner does not trigger it, and keeping the same owner does not excuse it.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-1157 requires every vehicle registered in Virginia and operated or parked on a highway to be inspected at an official inspection station, and § 46.2-1158 sets the schedule: within 12 months of the first inspection and at least once every 12 months thereafter. Each inspection is a complete one. If the car fails, the station issues a rejection sticker good for 15 calendar days, during which you can get the defect fixed and rechecked without being ticketed for that equipment problem. The Driver's Manual summarizes this as an annual safety inspection with a valid sticker displayed, and points to the Virginia State Police, which runs the program.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 7, p. 33 (Safety Inspections)

accuracy.note: § 46.2-1158: 'reinspected within 12 months of the month of the first inspection and at least once every 12 months thereafter'; rejection sticker 'valid for 15 calendar days beyond the day of issuance'. § 46.2-1157(A) sets the duty; subsection E (2020 Sp. Sess. I, effective 2021-03-01) bars a stop for an expired sticker until the first day of the fourth month after expiration; not used in the item. Manual p. 33: annual safety inspection, valid sticker, VSP website.

stem: Your car is kept at your home in Fairfax County. Besides the yearly safety inspection, what other inspection must it pass before DMV will register or renew it?

options.text: A separate tire-tread check by the State Police
options.rationale: Tread depth is already part of the safety inspection. Virginia has no stand-alone tire inspection.

options.text: An emissions inspection, which stays valid for two years
options.rationale: Correct. Vehicles garaged in the Northern Virginia program area must pass an emissions test, and DMV treats a passing result as good for two years.

options.text: An emissions inspection repeated every year along with the safety sticker
options.rationale: The two programs run on different clocks. The safety inspection is yearly; the emissions inspection is good for two years.

options.text: Nothing extra; emissions testing applies only to trucks over 8,500 pounds
options.rationale: It is the other way around. The enhanced program covers vehicles up to 10,000 pounds gross weight, which includes ordinary cars, and heavy trucks are outside it.

explanation: Virginia's enhanced emissions inspection program applies to vehicles of 10,000 pounds or less that are registered or mainly operated in the counties of Arlington, Fairfax, Loudoun, Prince William and Stafford and the cities of Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas and Manassas Park (Va. Code § 46.2-1178(C)). DMV will not register or renew a vehicle in that area until it has passed or been granted a repair-cost waiver, and a passing inspection is valid for two years. Vehicles more than 25 model years old and vehicles that run only on electricity or another clean fuel are exempt; qualifying hybrids skip the test but pay the program fee. Outside those localities, only the annual safety inspection applies.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 7, p. 33 (Safety Inspections)

accuracy.note: § 46.2-1178(C): enhanced program, vehicles 10,000 lb or less, model year less than 25 years old, in the five counties and five cities listed. DMV page: same locality list; 'Inspections are valid for two years'; no registration until passed or waived; clean-fuel-only vehicles exempt; qualifying hybrids pay the $2 per year fee without testing; 25-year age exemption. The 8,500 lb figure in distractor (d) is the weight cap in subsection A (the older basic program), which is why it is a plausible wrong answer. The two-year validity comes from DMV/DEQ, not the section text.

stem: You buy a used car from a neighbor for $6,000. When you go to DMV to put the title in your name, what tax will you owe on the purchase?

options.text: None; sales tax is collected only on dealer sales
options.rationale: The motor vehicle sales and use tax is due whenever ownership changes, and DMV collects it at titling. A private sale is not exempt.

options.text: 4.15% of the sale price, which is $249
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 58.1-2402 sets the rate at 4.15% of the sale price, and 4.15% of $6,000 is $249.

options.text: 6% of the sale price, the same as general retail sales tax
options.rationale: Cars have their own rate. Six percent is what the section charges for all-terrain vehicles and mopeds in some regions, not for a passenger car.

options.text: A flat $75, whatever the price
options.rationale: $75 is the floor, not the fee. You pay 4.15% of the price or $75, whichever is more, so on a $6,000 car the percentage wins.

explanation: Buying a car in Virginia comes with a motor vehicle sales and use tax of 4.15% of the sale price, with a minimum of $75 (Va. Code § 58.1-2402). DMV collects it when the title is transferred, whether you bought from a dealer or a private seller, so budget for it on top of the price. DMV computes it on the gross sales price after rebates; a trade-in credit does not lower the taxable amount, though a dealer's processing fee is included. On a $6,000 private sale that is $249, and you also have 30 days from the purchase to apply for the title.

authority.cite: Virginia DMV, Motor Vehicle Sales and Use Tax

accuracy.note: § 58.1-2402(A)(1): '4.15 percent beginning on and after July 1, 2016, of the sale price of each motor vehicle sold in Virginia'; minimum tax $75 on any vehicle taxed above zero percent; ATVs, mopeds and off-road motorcycles taxed at 6% or 5.3% depending on planning district. DMV page: 4.15% collected at titling whenever ownership changes; gross sales price or $75, whichever is greater; includes dealer processing fee, excludes trade-in credit. Arithmetic: 6000 x 0.0415 = 249.00. Section carries a contingent-expiration note (Acts 2019 c. 52) that does not alter the rate.

stem: Your family registers a fully electric car in Virginia. Which yearly charge shows up with its registration that the owner of a gas sedan getting 20 mpg does not pay?

options.text: A battery-disposal fee collected by DMV
options.rationale: Virginia collects no battery fee at registration. That confuses a possible future recycling cost with a charge that exists now.

options.text: A highway use fee, because the car pays little or no fuel tax
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-772 imposes an annual highway use fee on electric, alternative-fuel and fuel-efficient vehicles to make up for the fuel tax they avoid.

options.text: A higher personal property tax rate set by the state
options.rationale: Personal property tax on cars is set and billed by your city or county, not the state.

options.text: A surcharge for being exempt from emissions testing
options.rationale: Electric vehicles are exempt from the emissions test where it applies, and there is no charge attached to that exemption.

explanation: Virginia pays for roads partly through the tax on each gallon of fuel, so a car that burns little or none contributes less. To even that out, Va. Code § 46.2-772 adds an annual highway use fee at registration for electric vehicles, alternative-fuel vehicles and fuel-efficient vehicles, which DMV defines as a combined rating of 25 mpg or better. The amount is recalculated every July from what an average driver of a 23.7 mpg car would have paid in fuel tax; for electric vehicles DMV lists $135.63 for the year beginning July 1, 2026. Owners who drive less can instead enroll in the Mileage Choice program and pay per mile, capped at the flat fee. A 20 mpg gas sedan is below the threshold and owes nothing extra.

authority.cite: Virginia DMV, What is the Highway Use Fee?

accuracy.note: § 46.2-772(A): annual fee on any registered 'alternative fuel vehicle, an electric motor vehicle, or a fuel-efficient vehicle', collected at registration; (B) computed at 85% of the fuel tax a 23.7 mpg vehicle would pay over average annual miles, updated by July 1 each year; (C) exemptions for motorcycles, mopeds, autocycles, vehicles over 10,000 lb, government and IRP vehicles; $25 for low-speed vehicles; § 46.2-773 mileage-based alternative. DMV page: fuel-efficient means 25 mpg combined or greater; Mileage Choice option. The $135.63 EV figure for 2026-27 is from DMV's fee chart (HUF-fee-chart.pdf) and the highway-use page text; the number changes every July and should be re-checked then.

stem: It is 10 p.m. and a patrol car behind you turns on its emergency lights. You pull to the right and stop. What should you do about the lights inside your own car before the officer walks up?

options.text: Leave the cabin dark so the officer's flashlight is not washed out
options.rationale: Darkness hides your hands and everything in reach, which is exactly what makes an officer uneasy approaching a car at night. Light helps, it does not hinder.

options.text: Switch on the dome light so the officer can see inside
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual tells drivers stopped at night to turn on the interior light; a lit cabin lets the officer see you and your passengers and lowers the tension of the approach.

options.text: Flash your headlights a few times to show you noticed the stop
options.rationale: Your hazard flashers are the signal that you have seen the officer and are complying. Flashing headlights lights up the road, not your seats, and can confuse oncoming drivers.

options.text: Step out and stand by the rear bumper under the streetlight
options.rationale: Stay in the car unless the officer asks you to get out. Leaving the vehicle unprompted is read as a possible threat, day or night.

explanation: A traffic stop at night is harder on the officer than one in daylight because they cannot see what is inside your car. The Driver's Manual's traffic-stop checklist addresses that directly: after you have pulled over safely, put on your hazard flashers, and if it is dark, turn on the interior light. Then shut off the engine and anything noisy, lower the window, keep your belt on, and rest both hands where the officer can see them, ideally on the wheel. Every one of those steps makes you easier to read and the stop calmer for both sides.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 3, p. 26 (Traffic Stops)

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 3, p. 26 (Traffic Stops)

accuracy.note: Manual p. 26 traffic-stop list includes: turn on your flashers; if pulled over at night, turn on the vehicle's interior lights; stay in the vehicle unless asked; keep hands visible, preferably on the wheel; do not make movements that suggest reaching or hiding. No statute prescribes the interior light; this is manual procedure content, for which the Driver's Manual is the primary source.

stem: An officer writes you a summons for speeding and asks you to sign it. What does your signature mean?

options.text: You are admitting you committed the violation
options.rationale: Signing is not a guilty plea. You can still go to court, plead not guilty and argue your side; the signature says nothing about whether you did it.

options.text: You are promising to appear in court on the date shown, or otherwise resolve the ticket as the summons directs
options.rationale: Correct. Under Va. Code § 46.2-936 the summons is released on your written promise to appear; that promise is all the signature is.

options.text: You are giving up your right to a hearing before a judge
options.rationale: The opposite. The summons exists so you can have that hearing, and the statute even lets you demand one immediately or within 24 hours.

options.text: You are agreeing to pay the fine on the spot
options.rationale: Officers do not collect fines at the roadside. Payment, if any, happens later through the court, and only after you decide whether to contest the charge.

explanation: For a traffic infraction or misdemeanor under the motor vehicle laws, the officer takes your name, address and plate number and hands you a summons telling you when and where to appear (Va. Code § 46.2-936; § 46.2-937 applies the same procedure to infractions). Your signature is a written promise to show up, and once you give it the officer must release you. It is not an admission of anything, which is why the Driver's Manual tells you to sign it and save any disagreement for court. Since a 2021 amendment, refusing to sign no longer gets you arrested: the officer notes the refusal on the summons, tells you the court date and lets you go, but skipping that court date is a separate offense under § 46.2-938.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (April 2026), Section 3, p. 26 (Traffic Stops)

accuracy.note: § 46.2-936: officer issues a summons to appear at least five days out; right to an immediate hearing or one within 24 hours; 'Upon the giving by such person of his written promise to appear ... the officer shall forthwith release him'; if the person refuses to sign, the officer notes the refusal, gives notice of the hearing, 'and forthwith release[s] him from custody' (2021 Sp. Sess. I c. 338). Manual p. 26: sign the citation, it is not an admission of guilt, but it still says refusal may result in arrest, which is pre-2021 wording. The Code controls; the item's correct answer does not depend on the stale sentence.

stem: You are settling into the driver's seat before a trip and reach for the outside mirror controls. How should each side mirror be aimed?

options.text: So a wide strip of your own door and rear fender fills the inner half of the glass
options.rationale: Filling the mirror with your own car shrinks the view of the lane beside you, which is the part you need. The manual wants the car's side just barely in the picture, not dominating it.

options.text: So only a sliver of your car's side shows at the inner edge and the rest is the lane beside you
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual tells you to angle each side mirror until you can only just make out the side of your own vehicle, which pushes the view outward toward the blind area.

options.text: So it shows the road directly behind you, the same picture as the inside mirror
options.rationale: That duplicates what the inside mirror already covers. The inside mirror is set to frame the whole rear window; the side mirrors are for the areas the inside mirror cannot reach.

options.text: Tilted down toward the rear tires so you can watch the curb
options.rationale: Some drivers dip a mirror briefly for parallel parking, but that is not a driving setting. Aimed at the ground, the mirror shows nothing of the traffic beside you.

explanation: Mirrors get set before the car moves, and the Driver's Manual gives a simple test for the outside ones: turn each until you can only just see the side of your own vehicle. The inside mirror should frame the whole rear window. Set this way the three mirrors overlap as little as possible and cover more of the road beside and behind you, although a shoulder glance is still needed before changing lanes because no mirror setting removes the blind spot completely.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Blind Spots, p. 20

accuracy.note: Manual p. 20: adjust the inside mirror to frame the entire back window and both side mirrors so you can barely see the sides of the vehicle. The course's key on this topic (Session 4 p. 8) is the same direction of adjustment, phrased as seeing less of the vehicle. The effective date is the manual edition's PDF creation date (April 2026 edition); the manual carries no separate in-force date.

stem: Your car has antilock brakes (ABS). A dog darts into the road and you have to stop hard. To keep the wheels from locking, you should rapidly press and release the brake pedal.

options.text: True
options.rationale: Pumping is the technique for cars without antilock brakes, and it is exactly what the manual says not to do with ABS. The system already modulates the brakes for you; lifting off the pedal interrupts it and lengthens the stop.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual is blunt about it: never pump antilock brakes. Press the pedal and keep pressing; the pulsing you feel is the system working.

explanation: Antilock brakes exist so that a driver can brake hard without the wheels locking and skidding. The Driver's Manual tells you to learn how the system in your own car behaves, practice before you need it, and never pump the pedal. In an emergency you hold steady pressure and let the system do the rapid on-off work. The pedal may shudder or push back under your foot; that is normal and not a reason to let go.

source.basis: Course quizzes 10.1, 10.7 and 9.6 (ABS); Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Antilock Brakes, p. 15

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Antilock Brakes, p. 15

accuracy.note: Manual p. 15: understand how antilock brakes work, check the owner's manual, practice, and never pump antilock brakes. The manual states the prohibition only; the description of pedal pulsing and holding steady pressure in the rationale and explanation is general ABS operation, not a manual quotation.

stem: You park on a steep street facing uphill, with a curb along the passenger side of the car. Before you get out, which way do you turn the front wheels?

options.text: Toward the curb, so the tires rest against it
options.rationale: Turning toward the curb is the rule when you face downhill. Facing uphill, a car rolling backward with the wheels turned right would swing its rear end out into traffic instead of catching on the curb.

options.text: Away from the curb, so the back of the front tire can catch the curb if the car rolls
options.rationale: Correct. Facing uphill with a curb, turn the wheels left. If the parking brake fails and the car rolls back, the front tire rolls a few inches and jams against the curb.

options.text: Straight ahead, and rely on Park and the parking brake
options.rationale: Park and the parking brake are the first line of defense, but the manual still wants the wheels turned on a hill so that the curb becomes a backstop if both let go.

options.text: It makes no difference as long as the transmission is in Park
options.rationale: The manual gives a specific wheel direction for every hill-parking case precisely because Park alone can fail. Wheel position is a separate safeguard.

explanation: The Driver's Manual gives a wheel direction for each hill-parking situation. With a curb: facing downhill, turn the front wheels toward the curb (right); facing uphill, turn them away from the curb (left). With no curb, turn them toward the edge of the road (right) whether you face up or down, so that a rolling car heads away from traffic. The idea is the same every time: if the brakes give way, the car should move a short distance and stop against something, or at least leave the travel lane.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Parking on a hill, p. 22

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Parking on a hill, p. 22

accuracy.note: Manual p. 22 diagrams: downhill with curb, front wheels right; uphill with curb, front wheels left; downhill without curb, right; uphill without curb, right. Item keys the uphill-with-curb case only.

stem: You are reversing out of a driveway onto a quiet street. Where should you be looking for most of the maneuver?

options.text: At the inside mirror, which shows everything behind the car
options.rationale: No mirror shows everything. The manual's point is that mirrors leave gaps behind and beside the car, and the most common backing mistake is trusting them instead of turning around.

options.text: Switching between the two side mirrors
options.rationale: Side mirrors help at the edges, but the manual still wants your head and body turned so you see the full width of the space behind you through the glass, not a pair of narrow reflections.

options.text: Twisted round to the right, watching the space behind you through the back glass
options.rationale: Correct. Twist your upper body to the right so you are looking straight out the back glass, keep the car crawling, and keep flicking your eyes to each side for people and cars.

options.text: Straight ahead through the windshield so you can steer accurately
options.rationale: Facing forward means the whole area you are moving into is out of sight. Steering while backing is done by feel and by watching the rear, not the front.

explanation: The Driver's Manual says the most frequent error when reversing is not looking both ways behind the car. Mirrors do not give a complete picture, so the manual has you twist to the right and look directly out the rear window, keep the speed very low, and keep glancing to either side for pedestrians and approaching vehicles. A backup camera can help, but it does not replace turning around.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Backing, p. 22

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Backing, p. 22

accuracy.note: Manual p. 22, Backing: most common mistake is failing to look both ways behind; mirrors do not give a full view; turn body and head to the right and look through the rear window; back slowly and glance to either side. The backup-camera sentence in the explanation is not in the manual; it is added here as safe practice.

stem: Using clock numbers for spots on the steering wheel rim, which pair does the Virginia Driver's Manual give for a driver's two hands?

options.text: 10 and 2
options.rationale: This is the position many older drivers were taught, but it is not what the current manual recommends. Hands that high sit in front of the airbag and above the wheel's natural balance point.

options.text: 8 and 4
options.rationale: Correct. The manual puts the left hand at 8 o'clock and the right at 4, holding the rim with fingers and thumbs rather than gripping with the palms.

options.text: 12 and 6
options.rationale: One hand at the top and one at the bottom leaves you unable to turn far in either direction without crossing your arms, and it is not a position the manual describes.

options.text: One hand at 12, the other in your lap
options.rationale: A single hand on the wheel gives up half your control. The manual describes a two-handed position, sitting upright but relaxed.

explanation: The Driver's Manual describes a specific grip: sit up straight but relaxed, put your left hand where 8 o'clock would be and your right hand at 4 o'clock, and hold the rim with your fingers and thumbs instead of clamping it with your palms. The low position keeps your arms out of the airbag's path and lets you steer smoothly with small pulls rather than big shoulder movements.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Hand Position, p. 14

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Hand Position, p. 14

accuracy.note: Manual p. 14, Hand Position: sit straight but relaxed; hands at the 8 o'clock and 4 o'clock positions; hold with fingers and thumbs; avoid gripping with the palms. The airbag reasoning in the explanation is the course's stated rationale (Session 3), not the manual's; the manual gives the position without a reason.

stem: You have hitched a small utility trailer to the family SUV for the first time. Compared with the SUV on its own, how much longer should you expect passing, stopping, accelerating and turning to take?

options.text: About the same; a light trailer hardly changes how the vehicle behaves
options.rationale: Even a light trailer adds weight and length behind the rear axle, and the manual says it puts real extra stress on the tow vehicle. Treating it as no change is how drivers get caught out on the first hard stop.

options.text: Roughly half again as long
options.rationale: Closer, but still an underestimate. The manual's figure is a full doubling, not a 50 percent increase.

options.text: About twice as long
options.rationale: Correct. Doubling is the manual's rule of thumb for a light or medium trailer: passing, stopping, getting up to speed and turning all need roughly double the time and room.

options.text: Three to four times as long
options.rationale: That overstates it. The manual's guidance for light and medium trailers is a doubling; heavier combinations are a different topic.

explanation: Adding a trailer changes the load the vehicle has to move and stop. The Driver's Manual's rule of thumb for light and medium trailers is that every major maneuver takes about twice as long: twice the distance to pass, twice the room to stop, slower acceleration and wider, slower turns. So you need bigger gaps, earlier braking and extra lane length when changing lanes. If the trailer begins to sway, the manual's answer is to slow down.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Light to Medium Trailers, p. 21

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Light to Medium Trailers, p. 21

accuracy.note: Manual p. 21: towing a trailer places additional stress on the vehicle; it takes twice as long to pass, stop, accelerate and turn; allow for the added length when changing lanes; if the trailer sways, slow down.

stem: You are on an interstate at 60 mph on a dry afternoon. The car ahead passes an overpass shadow. Under the Driver's Manual's speed-based rule, how many seconds should you count before you reach that same shadow?

options.text: 2 seconds
options.rationale: Two seconds is the manual's figure for speeds below 35 mph. At 60 mph that gap is far too short to steer or brake out of trouble.

options.text: 3 seconds
options.rationale: Three seconds is the manual's number for the 35 to 45 mph band, and the flat rule many courses teach. At 60 mph the manual moves up to the next step.

options.text: 4 seconds
options.rationale: Correct. Between 46 and 70 mph the Driver's Manual calls for a four-second gap on a dry road.

options.text: 6 seconds
options.rationale: The manual has no six-second band. Extra seconds are added on top of the base figure for rain, heavy traffic or a poor road, not as the dry-pavement rule at 60 mph.

divergence: The course teaches one flat three-second gap for every speed (Session 6, page 21, question 6.9). The Driver's Manual scales the gap with speed: 2 seconds under 35 mph, 3 seconds from 35 to 45, 4 seconds from 46 to 70, and it warns that these cushions no longer work above 70. At 60 mph the manual's answer is 4 seconds; a course quiz phrased without a speed would accept 3.
explanation: The Driver's Manual's following-distance rule grows with speed. Watch the vehicle ahead pass a fixed mark, then count until you reach it: under 35 mph you need 2 seconds, from 35 to 45 mph 3 seconds, and from 46 to 70 mph 4 seconds. If you arrive before the count is up, drop back. Those are dry-road minimums; add time for rain, heavy traffic, a rough surface or a vehicle in poor condition. Above 70 mph the manual says the cushions no longer work.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Following Distance, p. 19

accuracy.note: Manual p. 19 table: 2 seconds under 35 mph, 3 seconds 35-45 mph, 4 seconds 46-70 mph; footnote that the cushions do not work above 70; add extra seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement or a vehicle in poor condition. Course question 6.9 keys a flat 3-second rule with no speed.

stem: You are passing a slow pickup on a two-lane road and are now alongside it in the oncoming lane. What tells you it is safe to move back to the right?

options.text: Your front bumper has drawn level with the pickup's front bumper
options.rationale: Level bumpers means you are still beside the truck. Pulling right now cuts across its nose, and a truck needs far more room to slow than a car.

options.text: You can see the pickup's entire front end in your inside rearview mirror
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual's test is that the whole front of the vehicle you passed appears in your rearview mirror; then there is room to return without crowding it.

options.text: The pickup's driver flashes the headlights at you
options.rationale: Some drivers do this as a courtesy, but it is not a signal you can count on and it is not what the manual tells you to judge by. Use your own mirror, not the other driver's habits.

options.text: You have been in the left lane for at least five seconds
options.rationale: Time in the passing lane says nothing about where the other vehicle is. The measure is the space you have opened up, read from the mirror.

explanation: A pass is not finished when you are ahead; it is finished when there is enough room to move over without forcing the passed driver to brake. The Driver's Manual gives one clear check: glance at your inside mirror and return to the right lane once the whole front of the passed vehicle is visible in it. Before the pass, check ahead, behind and your blind spot, signal, and accelerate; during it, stay within the speed limit; and never start a pass you cannot complete before a no-passing zone.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Passing, p. 17

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Passing, p. 17

accuracy.note: Manual p. 17, Passing: check traffic ahead, behind and in the blind spot; signal, then accelerate; return to the right lane once the front of the passed vehicle is visible in the rearview mirror; passing above the speed limit is illegal; complete the pass before a no-passing zone. The same mirror check is repeated for trucks on p. 21 (look for the entire front of the truck).

stem: Your turn signals have failed on the way home, so you signal with your arm out the driver's window. Which position tells other drivers you are about to turn right?

options.text: Left arm held straight out, level with your shoulder
options.rationale: A straight, horizontal left arm is the left-turn signal under Virginia law. It is the easy one to confuse because the arm points the way you will not be going.

options.text: Left arm bent at the elbow and pointing upward
options.rationale: Correct. Under Va. Code § 46.2-849 an arm extended upward from the driver's window means a right turn.

options.text: Left arm pointing downward
options.rationale: An arm pointing down means you are slowing or stopping, not turning.

options.text: Right arm held straight out of the passenger window
options.rationale: From the driver's seat a right arm out the far window cannot be seen by anyone who matters. The statute allows a right-arm signal only for people on bicycles, mopeds, e-bikes and similar devices.

explanation: Virginia law lists three arm signals a driver can give when the vehicle's lights are not used: the arm straight out and level for a left turn, the arm up for a right turn, and the arm down for slowing or stopping. All three are given with the left arm out the driver's window, because that is the side other drivers can see. Riders of bicycles, mopeds, e-bikes and scooters may instead stick the right arm straight out for a right turn. The Driver's Manual reproduces the same three signals with drawings.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Hand Signals, p. 18; Va. Code § 46.2-849

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Hand Signals, p. 18

accuracy.note: § 46.2-849 A: left turn, arm horizontal straight from and level with the shoulder; right turn, arm extended upward; slowing or stopping, arm extended downward. The same section lets a person on a bicycle, EPAMD, e-bike, moped or motorized skateboard/scooter signal a right turn with the right arm horizontal and stopping with the right arm down. Last amended 2019 c. 780, hence effective 2019-07-01. Manual p. 18 shows the three signals as left-arm drawings. The manual's sample exam (Section 8, q8) asks about the stop signal; this item asks about the right-turn signal with different wording.

stem: On a two-lane country road a car is sitting right on your rear bumper, and there is no second lane to move into. What does the Driver's Manual suggest you do?

options.text: Touch the brake pedal lightly so your brake lights flash, and gradually ease off your speed
options.rationale: Correct. A gentle brake tap warns the driver behind without slowing you sharply, and easing down encourages them to pass or back off.

options.text: Brake hard once to make the other driver back off
options.rationale: A sudden stop in front of someone who is too close is the setup for a rear-end crash, which is the very collision tailgating produces. The manual says specifically not to brake suddenly.

options.text: Speed up to open a gap between you
options.rationale: Now you are speeding and the tailgater simply follows. The gap that matters is the one behind you, and you cannot create it by going faster.

options.text: Hold your speed exactly and ignore the other car; the gap is their problem
options.rationale: The gap is their fault, but the crash would involve you too. The manual wants you to act: slow gently, signal with the lights, and let them past.

explanation: Tailgating is another driver following you too closely. Because a hard stop would put their bumper into yours, the Driver's Manual tells you not to brake suddenly. Instead, change lanes if there is one, or tap the brake pedal gently so the brake lights flash and then slow down gradually; both invite the tailgater to pass or drop back. The same idea works the other way round: keep a steady speed and a safe gap yourself, and tap the brakes early to warn the driver behind when you are about to slow or stop.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Following Distance (tailgating), p. 19

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Following Distance, p. 19

accuracy.note: Manual p. 19: tailgating is following too closely; if tailgated, do not brake suddenly; if possible move to another lane, or gently tap the brakes to flash the brake lights and slow down, which should encourage the tailgater to pass or slow; help the driver behind by keeping a safe gap and steady speed, and tap the brakes to warn when slowing or stopping.

stem: You reach a four-way crossing in a neighborhood that has no signs, signals, or painted markings at the same moment as another car coming from the street on your right. Under Virginia law, who goes first?

options.text: You, because your bumper was slightly ahead
options.rationale: Reaching the crossing at roughly the same time is exactly the case the statute settles, and it does not settle it in your favor. A clear gap in arrival lets the earlier car go; a near-tie hands the road to the driver on the right.

options.text: The other driver, because the car on the right has priority
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-820 puts the duty to yield on the driver on the left whenever two vehicles reach an uncontrolled intersection at about the same time.

options.text: Whichever car is on the wider street
options.rationale: Road width plays no part in the rule; it is a guess people make from feel. Only a sign or signal changes the default, and this crossing has neither.

options.text: The car going straight, over one that is turning
options.rationale: That tiebreaker belongs to a left turn across oncoming traffic under § 46.2-825. It does not decide a meeting between two cars arriving from cross streets.

explanation: When nothing controls an intersection, Virginia's default rule in Va. Code § 46.2-820 is short: if two cars arrive at about the same time, the one on the left waits for the one on the right. If one driver is plainly there first, that driver goes. Neither the size of the street nor who is turning changes that at a plain four-way meeting of cross streets. Slow down on the approach so that a near-tie is easy to recognize and easy to give way in.

accuracy.note: § 46.2-820 text: when two vehicles approach or enter an uncontrolled intersection at approximately the same time, the driver on the left yields to the vehicle on the right. Last amended 1989 c. 727 (the Title 46.2 recodification). The 07-01 date follows the default convention; the recodification act may carry its own effective date (possibly 1989-10-01) which could not be confirmed on LIS. § 46.2-825 (left-turn yield) is cited only to anchor the rationale for option d.

stem: It is late at night and the traffic light on your road has switched to a flashing yellow, while the cross street faces a flashing red. What does the flashing yellow require of you?

options.text: Stop completely first, then continue once nothing is coming
options.rationale: That is the meaning of the flashing red on the cross street, which works like a stop sign. It is not what your signal says, and an unexpected stop on the main road invites a rear-end collision.

options.text: Ease off, check both ways, and continue through without stopping
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-833 says a flashing circular amber lets traffic go through the intersection or past the signal with reasonable care under the circumstances.

options.text: Stop and wait for the light to cycle to green
options.rationale: A flashing signal is not cycling; there is no green coming. Waiting for one is the classic late-night mistake at a flasher.

options.text: Keep your normal speed; the flash only means the signal is switched off
options.rationale: The signal is not off, and reasonable care is not normal speed. Cross traffic is stopping and then entering, so you must be ready for it.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-833 assigns every light a meaning. A flashing circular yellow tells you to proceed with reasonable care for the conditions: reduce speed, look both ways, expect cross traffic. A flashing circular red tells you to stop before entering the intersection, exactly as at a stop sign, and then go when it is safe. Signals often switch to this pairing overnight, with the busier road getting the yellow, so whichever color you face, the cross street is facing the other one.

accuracy.note: Subsection A: 'Flashing circular amber indicates that traffic may proceed through the intersection or past such signal with reasonable care under the circumstances'; 'Flashing circular red indicates that traffic shall stop before entering an intersection.' Latest amendment 2013 cc. 128, 400. The Driver's Manual (Section 2, p. 5) states the same for both colors.

stem: You are stuck behind a slow tractor on a two-lane country road as it climbs toward the top of a hill you cannot see over. If you pull into the oncoming lane to get past before the crest, how does Virginia classify that?

options.text: Legal, as long as no car is visible coming the other way
options.rationale: Seeing nobody is the whole problem: the hill hides the oncoming lane, so an empty view proves nothing. The statute bans the pass where your sight line is blocked, whatever you happen to see.

options.text: A minor traffic infraction with a small fine
options.rationale: An ordinary lane or speed slip is an infraction. A blind pass on a hill sits in the reckless-driving article of the Code, a criminal charge rather than a ticket.

options.text: Reckless driving
options.rationale: Correct. Overtaking while on or approaching the crest of a grade, or a curve, where the view ahead is obstructed is one of the acts Va. Code § 46.2-854 names as reckless driving, unless each direction has two or more lanes.

options.text: Legal on any road provided you finish the pass quickly
options.rationale: How fast you finish never makes it lawful. The statute's exception is about the road, not the driver: two or more lanes in each direction, or a one-way roadway.

explanation: Virginia lists specific acts that count as reckless driving, and Va. Code § 46.2-854 makes one of them passing another vehicle while on or approaching the top of a hill, or on or approaching a curve, where you cannot see far enough along the road. Reckless driving is a criminal offense, far heavier than a routine ticket.
