The rule does not apply on a highway with at least two marked lanes in your direction or on a one-way road, because there you are not moving into an oncoming lane to pass.

accuracy.note: Section text: reckless driving to overtake and pass another vehicle proceeding in the same direction on or approaching the crest of a grade or a curve where the driver's view along the highway is obstructed, except on a highway with two or more designated lanes per direction or a designated one-way roadway. Last amended 1989 c. 727 (recodification); the 07-01 date follows the default convention and the act's own effective date could not be confirmed on LIS. The Driver's Manual (Section 3, p. 17) lists hills and curves among places where passing is unlawful.

stem: You are on a county road well outside any town when the crossing gate at a railroad track ahead starts to come down. Where does Virginia law require you to stop?

options.text: Anywhere behind the gate arm, even right up against it
options.rationale: Stopping at the arm itself can put you inside the 15-foot band next to the rail. The statute sets a minimum gap from the track, not merely a place behind the gate.

options.text: Somewhere from 15 to 50 feet short of the closest rail
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-885 fixes both ends of the band: no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet, measured from the nearest rail.

options.text: At least 100 feet back from the track
options.rationale: One hundred feet is the signaling distance for a turn or lane change where the speed limit is over 35 mph. It is not the railroad rule, and stopping that far back can leave you beyond where the crossing equipment is meant to hold traffic.

options.text: Somewhere from 5 to 20 feet short of the closest rail
options.rationale: Five feet is well inside the minimum. The numbers sound close, but the statute's band starts at 15 feet, not 5.

explanation: When a gate is lowering, a signal is flashing, a flagger is stopping traffic, or a train is plainly close, Va. Code § 46.2-885 tells you to stop no nearer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, and to stay there until you can cross safely. The same section makes it illegal to drive through, around, or under a gate that is down or moving. The stated band is written for roads outside cities and towns, which is why this question puts you on a county road; the safe habit is the same everywhere.

accuracy.note: Subsection A opens 'Except in cities or towns' and requires a stop 'within 50 feet but not less than 15 feet from the nearest rail' when a signal warns of a train, a gate is lowered or a flagman signals, a train sounds its signal, or an approaching train is plainly visible and hazardous. Subsection B bans driving through, around, or under a closed or moving gate. Latest amendment 2012 c. 828. Note § 46.2-884 is a different section (disobeying a crossing signal); do not cite it for the distance.

stem: You are on I-95 at 65 mph and want to move one lane to the left. For how far must your turn signal be on before you begin the lane change?

options.text: At least 50 feet
options.rationale: Fifty feet is the requirement where the lawful speed is 35 mph or less. On an interstate the longer distance applies.

options.text: At least 100 feet
options.rationale: Correct. Where the lawful speed is more than 35 mph, Va. Code § 46.2-849 requires the signal to run continuously for at least 100 feet before turning, partly turning, slowing, or stopping.

options.text: At least 200 feet
options.rationale: A doubled figure people assume for highway speed. The statute has a single threshold at 35 mph, and 100 feet is the only longer distance it sets.

options.text: There is no minimum; the signal only has to be on before you move
options.rationale: The law is specific about distance, not merely timing. A flick of the stalk as you steer over does not satisfy it.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-849 ties the signaling distance to the lawful speed: at least 100 feet where it is more than 35 mph, at least 50 feet everywhere else. A lane change is a partial turn out of your straight line, so the signal rule applies to it just as it does to a turn at a corner. At 65 mph you cover 100 feet in about a second, so the practical version is: signal early, check mirrors and blind spot, then move.

accuracy.note: § 46.2-849(B): 'Wherever the lawful speed is more than 35 miles per hour, such signals shall be given continuously for a distance of at least 100 feet, and in all other cases at least 50 feet, before slowing down, stopping, turning, or partly turning.' Latest amendment 2019 c. 780. § 46.2-848 is the duty to signal when another vehicle may be affected; its 'partly turn from a direct line' wording is what brings a lane change under the rule. The course states a flat 100 feet for lane changes (Session 2, page 52), which matches the law at expressway speed but omits the 50-foot tier.

stem: On a three-lane stretch of interstate you are comfortable at 60 mph while most traffic is moving faster. Which lane does Virginia law say you belong in?

options.text: The middle lane, so faster cars can get by on either side
options.rationale: Being overtaken on both sides is what the rule is meant to prevent. The middle lane is for through traffic keeping pace, not for the slowest vehicle on the road.

options.text: The left lane, as long as you hold a steady speed
options.rationale: The left lane is for overtaking. Sitting in it below the flow is also what Va. Code § 46.2-842.1 targets: on a divided highway you must move right for a vehicle coming up to pass.

options.text: The far right lane, beside the road's edge
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-804 requires a vehicle traveling below the normal speed of traffic to use the right-hand lane, except when passing, preparing to turn left, or where signs assign lanes differently.

options.text: Any lane, because you are at or under the speed limit
options.rationale: The rule keys on the speed of the traffic around you, not on the posted limit. Being legal on speed does not make the left or middle lane yours.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-804 says a vehicle moving slower than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place must be driven in the lane nearest the right edge of the road, with exceptions for overtaking, setting up a left turn, and lanes reserved by signs. A second rule, § 46.2-842.1, adds that on a divided highway you may not hang in the left lane beside another car while someone is trying to pass; you move right as soon as it is safe. On an expressway the left lane is a passing lane, the right lane is where slower traffic lives, and the middle carries the through flow.

accuracy.note: § 46.2-804(1): any vehicle proceeding at less than the normal speed of traffic 'shall be driven in the lane nearest the right edge or right curb of the highway when such lane is available for travel except when overtaking and passing another vehicle or in preparation for a left turn or where right lanes are reserved for slow-moving traffic'. Latest amendment 2017 c. 795. § 46.2-842.1 (latest 2020 c. 815): unlawful to fail to give way to overtaking traffic when driving to the left and abreast of another vehicle on a divided highway. The Driver's Manual (Section 3, p. 17) states the same practice: right lane when slower, left lane for passing only.

stem: On a street with two lanes in your direction, the car in the lane beside you has stopped at a marked crosswalk for someone crossing. Can you drive past it?

options.text: Yes, if the person crossing has not yet reached your lane
options.rationale: This mixes up the trigger for your own stop (a pedestrian in your lane, or in the next lane heading toward it) with the separate ban in subsection B, which forbids passing a vehicle that has stopped for a pedestrian at all.

options.text: Yes, if you slow to a crawl and are ready to brake
options.rationale: Slowing is not the standard. The stopped car hides the person crossing from you, which is exactly why the law takes the choice away.

options.text: No; you may not overtake a vehicle that is stopped for a pedestrian at a crosswalk
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-924(B) bars any driver approaching from an adjacent lane or from behind from passing a vehicle that has stopped under the crosswalk rule.

options.text: Yes, provided you sound your horn first
options.rationale: A horn warns; it grants no right to pass. Nothing in the pedestrian statute lets a signal stand in for stopping.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-924 makes a driver stop for a pedestrian who is in the driver's lane, or in the next lane and heading toward it, at a marked crosswalk, at the ordinary crossing at the end of a block, or at any intersection on a road posted 35 mph or lower. Subsection B closes the obvious loophole: once a vehicle has stopped for that pedestrian, nobody approaching from behind or from a neighbouring lane may overtake it. A car stopped at a crosswalk is a signal that someone is crossing where you cannot see them. Breaking the rule is a traffic infraction, and if a pedestrian is seriously hurt or killed it becomes a Class 1 misdemeanor.

accuracy.note: Subsection B: 'When a vehicle is stopped pursuant to subsection A, the driver of any other vehicle approaching from an adjacent lane or from behind the stopped vehicle shall not overtake and pass such stopped vehicle.' Subsection A lists the three crossing types and the 35-mph intersection condition, and grades the violation as an infraction, or a Class 1 misdemeanor where a vulnerable road user is seriously injured or killed. Latest amendment 2025 c. 447; what that act changed was not determined; subsection B predates it (it appears in the 2020 c. 1031 rewrite). The Driver's Manual (Section 3, p. 20) states passing at a crosswalk is illegal.

stem: You catch up to someone riding a bicycle along the right edge of a two-lane road. What is the smallest gap Virginia allows between your car and the bike as you go by?

options.text: Eighteen inches, roughly the width of an open car door
options.rationale: A door's width feels like room from the driver's seat, but it is half the legal minimum. At that distance a wobble or a gust puts the rider under your mirror.

options.text: Three feet
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-839 requires passing at a reasonable speed at least three feet to the left of a bicycle, moped, animal, or animal-drawn vehicle, and says to change lanes if your lane is too narrow to manage that.

options.text: Five feet
options.rationale: Five feet is more room than the statute demands. Giving it is a fine habit, but the question asks for the legal floor, and that is three.

options.text: Whatever fits inside your lane, since you may not leave it to pass a bike
options.rationale: Backwards. If the lane is too narrow for the required gap, the statute tells you to move into the other lane rather than squeeze by.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-839 sets the rule for overtaking a bicycle, an electric bike, a moped, a ridden animal, or a horse-drawn vehicle: pass at a reasonable speed with at least three feet between you and them, and do not drift back to the right until you are safely clear. If your lane is not wide enough to leave three feet while staying in it, the same section tells you to change lanes to pass. A cyclist can wobble, swerve around a pothole, or be pushed sideways by wind, so treat three feet as the floor and give more when you can.

source.basis: Session 6 quiz 6.12 (three-foot passing rule); Session 10, page 69 (passing bicyclists)

accuracy.note: Section text: a driver overtaking a bicycle, EPAMD, electric power-assisted bicycle, moped, animal, or animal-drawn vehicle 'shall pass at a reasonable speed at least three feet to the left' and 'shall not again proceed to the right side of the highway until safely clear'; 'If the lane of travel is not wide enough ... the overtaking vehicle shall change lanes.' Latest amendment 2021 Sp. Sess. I c. 462 (the change-lanes sentence). The Driver's Manual (Section 3, pp. 17 and 20) states the three-foot rule the same way.

stem: You are overtaking a tractor-trailer on the interstate. What tells you it is safe to move back into the lane ahead of it?

options.text: The truck's headlights are level with your rear bumper
options.rationale: At that point the cab is beside you and you are inside the truck's front blind spot, which can reach about 20 feet ahead of the cab. Pulling in there sets up a rear-end crash the truck cannot avoid.

options.text: The truck's whole front end is visible in your rearview mirror
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual gives exactly this cue: the entire front of the rig showing in your rearview mirror before you pull in, and then keep your speed up.

options.text: You have been in the left lane for at least ten seconds
options.rationale: Time is not the test; distance is. A rig can be 65 feet long and getting past one can take more than half a mile, so a clock tells you nothing about where its nose is.

options.text: The truck driver flashes the headlights at you
options.rationale: Some drivers do flash as a courtesy, but it is neither a rule nor what the manual tells you to rely on. Your own mirror check is the standard.

explanation: A loaded truck needs close to twice the time and room to stop that a car does, so cutting in front of one and then easing off is one of the surest ways to be hit from behind. The Virginia Driver's Manual (Section 3, Sharing the Road, p. 21) says to finish the pass, check your rearview mirror for the full front of the truck, and only then move over, keeping your speed steady. The manual also gives the size of the problem: blind spots up to about 20 feet ahead of the cab and roughly 200 feet behind the trailer, plus wide zones down both sides.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Sharing the Road, p. 21

accuracy.note: Manual p. 21, 'Front No-Zone': trucks, buses and RVs need nearly twice the time and room to stop as cars; a truck and trailer may be as long as 65 feet and may take more than half a mile to pass; when passing, look for the entire front of the truck in the rearview mirror before pulling in front, then maintain speed. 'Wide Turns': blind spots may stretch up to 20 feet in front of the cab and approximately 200 feet behind. The 'effective' date is the PDF's creation date for the April 2026 edition; there is no statute behind this procedure.

stem: You are first in line when your light turns green, but a funeral procession led by a sheriff's car is still crossing in front of you against its red. What should you do?

options.text: Go, because a green light gives you the right-of-way over the procession
options.rationale: An escorted procession keeps the right-of-way on any road it uses, green light or not, under Va. Code § 46.2-828. The signal does not override that.

options.text: Wait until the last vehicle in the procession has cleared the intersection
options.rationale: Correct. The procession has the right-of-way, and no outside vehicle may pass through it or interfere with it.

options.text: Slip into a gap in the procession if there is room
options.rationale: Entering a gap is passing through the procession, which the statute forbids, and doing it deliberately is an infraction that carries four demerit points under § 46.2-828.1.

options.text: Turn on your hazard lights and follow the last car through
options.rationale: Flashing hazards are how procession vehicles identify themselves; switching yours on to tag along is joining the procession, which is also prohibited.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 46.2-828 a funeral procession traveling under police or sheriff's escort has the right-of-way on every road it uses, and no outside vehicle may join it, pass through it, or interfere with it. Vehicles in the procession may run high beams and flash all four turn signals, which is how you can tell where it ends. Deliberately impeding or disrupting an escorted procession is a traffic infraction that adds four demerit points to your record under § 46.2-828.1. So when one crosses against your green, hold your position until the last car is through, then go.

accuracy.note: § 46.2-828: processions under police or sheriff's escort 'shall have the right-of-way in any highway through which they may pass'; procession vehicles may display high beams and flash all four turn signals or hazard lights; 'No vehicle that is not properly part of a funeral procession shall join, pass through, or interfere with the passage of any funeral procession under escort'. Latest amendment 2012 c. 26. § 46.2-828.1(A): intentionally impeding or disrupting a procession is a traffic infraction plus four demerit points; (B) applies only to processions under police/sheriff escort or led by vehicles with warning lights under § 46.2-1025. Enacted 2000 c. 274. The statutory right-of-way is tied to an escort, which is why the stem includes the sheriff's car.

stem: A driver finished several drinks about an hour ago and wants to get behind the wheel. Which of these is the one thing that actually lowers the alcohol in the bloodstream?

options.text: A strong cup of coffee
options.rationale: Caffeine can make a drinker feel more awake, but it removes no alcohol from the blood. An alert drunk is still a drunk, and still impaired.

options.text: A cold shower
options.rationale: Cold water shocks the skin, not the liver. The body keeps clearing alcohol at its own fixed pace no matter how awake the shower makes someone feel.

options.text: Waiting long enough for the body to process the alcohol
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual is blunt about it: nothing but time brings intoxication down. Coffee, cold water, and exercise are all listed as things that do not work.

options.text: Twenty minutes of hard exercise
options.rationale: Sweating does not burn off alcohol. The manual names exercise alongside coffee and cold showers as a method that fails to sober anyone up.

explanation: Alcohol leaves the body at a steady rate that no home remedy speeds up. The Virginia Driver's Manual (Section 3, Drunk and Drugged Driving, p. 24) states that time is the only thing that reduces intoxication, and it specifically rules out coffee, cold showers, and exercise. It also warns that a single drink already affects vision, judgment, and coordination, so the safe plan is to not drive at all after drinking rather than to try to sober up quickly.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, Drunk and Drugged Driving, p. 24

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, p. 24

accuracy.note: Manual p. 24, Drunk and Drugged Driving: one sentence says only time decreases intoxication and that coffee, cold showers, and exercise do not. The preceding paragraph confirms one drink affects vision, judgment, and coordination. No statute states a sobering rate; the item deliberately avoids any per-hour figure.

stem: You are 17 and taking a medicine your doctor prescribed. It makes you drowsy, you drive anyway, and an officer stops you for weaving across the lane. Can you be charged with DUI when the drug was legal for you to take?

options.text: No. DUI covers alcohol and illegal drugs only.
options.rationale: Va. Code § 18.2-266 clause (iii) reaches any self-administered intoxicant or drug of any kind that impairs driving. Whether the drug was lawful to take is beside the point; what matters is the impairment.

options.text: Yes. Any drug, prescribed or over the counter, that impairs your ability to drive safely can support a DUI charge.
options.rationale: Correct. The statute does not ask where the drug came from. A prescription bottle is not a defense if the medicine makes you unfit to drive, and the manual says drug impairment carries the same penalties as alcohol DUI.

options.text: Only if your blood alcohol concentration is also 0.08 or more.
options.rationale: The 0.08 figure is the alcohol per se rule in clause (i). Drug impairment under clause (iii) needs no alcohol in the picture at all.

options.text: Only if the drug is one of the four on Virginia's per se blood-level list.
options.rationale: Cocaine, methamphetamine, PCP, and MDMA have fixed blood thresholds in clause (v), but that is one route to a conviction. Clause (iii) separately covers impairment by any other drug, with no threshold needed.

explanation: Virginia's DUI statute, Va. Code § 18.2-266, lists several independent ways to commit the offense. Clause (iii) makes it unlawful to drive under the influence of any narcotic or any other self-administered intoxicant or drug of any nature, to a degree that impairs safe driving. Nothing in that clause distinguishes a prescription from a street drug. The Driver's Manual (Section 3, p. 24-25) says the same thing in plain words: if a drug impairs your driving, the penalties match those for alcohol, and it warns that ordinary cold, allergy, and headache medicines can cause the drowsiness and slowed reactions that get you there.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, p. 24-25

accuracy.note: § 18.2-266 clause (iii): 'under the influence of any narcotic drug or any other self-administered intoxicant or drug of whatsoever nature, or any combination of such drugs, to a degree which impairs his ability to drive'; clause (iv) covers combined alcohol and drugs; clause (v) is the per se list (cocaine 0.02 mg/L, meth 0.1, PCP 0.01, MDMA 0.1). History line ends 2005. Manual p. 24: drug impairment 'may face the same penalties' as alcohol DUI; p. 25: over-the-counter and prescription medicines can cause drowsiness and dizziness. Option c uses the 'or more' formulation deliberately (CS-05).

stem: You are 17 and heading to a party where you know there will be drinking. According to the Virginia Driver's Manual, when is the right moment to settle how you will get home safely?

options.text: Before you go, by lining up a sober driver or another way home.
options.rationale: Correct. The manual's advice is to make the no-driving decision before the first drink and to arrange the ride in advance, because alcohol erodes exactly the judgment you would need to make that call later.

options.text: After your first drink, once you can tell how it is affecting you.
options.rationale: Judgment is among the first things alcohol dulls. The manual notes that choosing not to drive becomes much harder once one or two drinks are in you, which is why the decision has to come first.

options.text: At the end of the night, based on whether you feel fine to drive.
options.rationale: Feeling fine is not a measurement. Even a single drink affects vision and coordination, and an impaired brain is a poor judge of its own impairment.

options.text: Only if you hear that police have a checkpoint nearby.
options.rationale: The reason to plan a ride is the crash risk, which the manual puts at seven times higher after drinking, not the chance of being caught.

explanation: The Driver's Manual (Section 3, Drunk and Drugged Driving, p. 24-25) frames alcohol-related crashes as preventable, and the way to prevent them is to decide before drinking starts that you will not drive, then arrange alternative transportation or a sober driver ahead of the event. The order matters because alcohol attacks judgment first: the same person who would plan sensibly while sober is much less likely to do so after a drink or two. For an under-21 driver the stakes include the Zero Tolerance law, where a BAC as low as 0.02 costs a year of driving.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, Drunk and Drugged Driving, p. 24-25

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, p. 24-25

accuracy.note: Manual p. 24: crashes are preventable; the only way to avoid the risk is to decide before drinking that you will not drive; the decision is harder after one or two drinks; crash odds seven times greater after drinking. Manual p. 25: at a social event where alcohol is served, plan ahead for a sober ride using alternative transportation or a sober driver. The 0.02 Zero Tolerance reference in the explanation is § 18.2-266.1, already verified in the bank (de10a-zero-tolerance).

stem: A 20-year-old is convicted of DUI in Virginia. A 15-year-old friend was in the passenger seat at the time. What does the passenger's age add to the driver's sentence?

options.text: Nothing. A passenger's age only matters if there was a crash.
options.rationale: Va. Code § 18.2-270(D) triggers on transporting a person 17 or younger during the offense. No crash, injury, or complaint is required.

options.text: An extra fine of $500 to $1,000 plus at least five days in jail.
options.rationale: Correct. Section 18.2-270(D) adds a mandatory fine in that range and a mandatory minimum five days of confinement on top of the ordinary DUI penalty whenever the offense was committed with a passenger aged 17 or younger.

options.text: A one-year license suspension for the passenger.
options.rationale: The passenger broke no law by riding along. The enhancement punishes the driver, not the person put at risk.

options.text: An extra $250 minimum fine.
options.rationale: $250 is the mandatory minimum fine every first DUI carries under § 18.2-270(A). The child-passenger enhancement is a separate, larger amount stacked on top of it.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 18.2-270, a first DUI is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a mandatory minimum $250 fine, and higher BACs bring mandatory jail. Subsection D adds a specific enhancement for endangering a child: a driver convicted of DUI while carrying a passenger aged 17 or younger is fined an additional $500 to $1,000 and must serve a mandatory minimum of five days in jail. The Driver's Manual (Section 5, p. 30) describes the same rule. For a teen driver that passenger is usually a friend, which makes this one of the most likely DUI enhancements to apply.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 5, p. 30

accuracy.note: § 18.2-270(D) read on LIS: 'committed while transporting a person 17 years of age or younger shall be (i) fined an additional minimum of $500 and not more than $1,000 and (ii) sentenced to a mandatory minimum period of confinement of five days.' Subsection A: Class 1 misdemeanor, mandatory minimum fine $250; BAC 0.15-0.20 adds 5 days, above 0.20 adds 10. History line ends 2014, c. 707. The manual p. 30 also mentions an 80-hour community service add-on for a second offense with a juvenile aboard; that sentence is not in § 18.2-270(D) as published, so the item stays on the first-offense enhancement.

stem: Virginia DMV hands out a blue envelope that a driver keeps with the registration and insurance card. Which drivers is it designed to help during a traffic stop?

options.text: Drivers on the autism spectrum, so the officer knows they may communicate differently and need a calm approach.
options.rationale: Correct. The program was created by Va. Code § 46.2-203.3 for exactly this group. The envelope tells the officer about the diagnosis, offers interaction guidance, and holds the documents so the driver is not fumbling for them under stress.

options.text: Teen drivers facing their first-ever traffic stop.
options.rationale: Every new driver finds a first stop nerve-racking, but the envelope is aimed at a specific communication need rather than at inexperience. Anyone can reduce stress by knowing the routine in advance; the envelope is not a beginner's tool.

options.text: Drivers with a hearing or vision impairment.
options.rationale: A sensible guess, since those drivers may also communicate differently, but the statute names autism spectrum disorder specifically. Other needs are handled through different DMV programs.

options.text: Drivers with a past DUI who want to show the officer they are sober.
options.rationale: The envelope carries communication guidance and documents, not a driving record, and has nothing to do with sobriety.

explanation: Traffic stops are stressful for anyone, and for a driver on the autism spectrum flashing lights, loud commands, and unexpected questions can make communicating much harder. Virginia's Driver Communication Improvement Program, better known as the Blue Envelope Program, was set up under Va. Code § 46.2-203.3 (effective July 1, 2025). A participating driver picks up the envelope free at any DMV customer service center, with no documentation required, and stores the registration, insurance, and emergency contact inside. When handed to an officer it signals the diagnosis and gives the officer guidance on a patient, clear interaction. Participation is voluntary and confidential.

accuracy.note: § 46.2-203.3 (2025, c. 665): Department shall develop a program to print and distribute envelopes for drivers diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder as defined in § 38.2-3418.17; envelope may carry a diagnosis statement, law-enforcement interaction guidelines, space for communication needs, and directions to keep registration, insurance, and emergency contact inside. DMV page: voluntary, confidential, free, no documentation required, available at any customer service center, helps during stops or crashes. The course's own heading for this material is 'Reducing stress and anxiety during traffic stops', which is why it sits under DE.11a.

stem: Another car squeezes in front of you with almost no room and you feel your temper flare. Which reaction stops that anger from turning into aggressive driving?

options.text: Close the gap and ride the other car's bumper so the driver gets the message.
options.rationale: Following too closely is one of the behaviors the Driver's Manual lists for drivers venting anger on the road. It is also one of the offenses named in Va. Code § 46.2-868.1, and tailgating that makes you a hazard to the other driver is aggressive driving on its own, whether or not you meant any harm.

options.text: Flash your high beams and lean on the horn.
options.rationale: The manual names flashing lights and honking among the things angry drivers do. It escalates the situation instead of ending it.

options.text: Ease off, let the space in front open back up, and let it go.
options.rationale: Correct. Backing off restores your following distance and removes you from the confrontation. The manual's advice around hostile drivers is to stay out of their way and not take the bait.

options.text: Draw level with the other car and stare the driver down.
options.rationale: The manual says to avoid eye contact and ignore gestures when an aggressive driver is nearby. A stare-down is an invitation to escalate, and it takes your attention off the road.

explanation: The Driver's Manual (Section 3, Aggressive Driving, p. 23) describes what anger looks like behind the wheel: tailgating, weaving, honking, flashing lights, shouting, and hand gestures. It also explains the risk: those drivers put their own frustration ahead of everyone else's safety. Va. Code § 46.2-868.1 turns that into a crime in two steps. First, the driver commits one of a list of offenses, including following too closely, unsafe passing, ignoring lane markings, speeding, and failing to give way to an overtaking vehicle. Second, either that driving makes the person a hazard to someone else, or the offense is committed with intent to harass, intimidate, injure, or obstruct another person. Being a hazard is enough by itself; no proof of intent is needed. Aggressive driving is a Class 2 misdemeanor, and intent matters only as the aggravator: with intent to injure it becomes a Class 1 misdemeanor, and the court may also order an aggressive driving program. Managing anger means noticing the flare-up and choosing the boring response: more space, no signals back, and moving on. The same manual page advises staying clear of an aggressive driver and avoiding eye contact, which works just as well when the anger is your own.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, Aggressive Driving, p. 23

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, p. 23

accuracy.note: Manual p. 23: aggressive drivers take out their anger on other motorists; behaviors listed include tailgating, weaving, passing on the right, unsafe lane changes, gestures, screaming, honking, flashing lights; advice is to stay out of the way, not challenge by speeding up or out-maneuvering, avoid eye contact, ignore gestures and shouting. § 46.2-868.1(A), re-read on LIS 2026-09-04: guilty if (i) the person violates a listed section (§ 46.2-802, -804, -816 following too closely, -821, -833.1, -838, -841, -842, -842.1, -843, any Article 8 speed provision, or -888) AND (ii) 'that person is a hazard to another person OR commits an offense in clause (i) with the intent to harass, intimidate, injure or obstruct another person'. Hazard is a prong of its own; intent is not required for the offense. (B): Class 2 misdemeanor; with intent to injure, Class 1; court may require an aggressive driving program. History 2002, cc. 752, 782. CX-02 (course says intent required in one session, not in the other): the statute answers it, and this item now states both prongs.

stem: Two hours into a late-night drive you notice your eyelids drooping and cannot remember the last few exits. Which of these actually reduces the danger?

options.text: Cracking a window and turning the music up.
options.rationale: The Driver's Manual lists both fresh air and loud music as things that do not keep a sleepy driver awake. They may cover the drowsiness for a minute, then it comes back.

options.text: Downing an energy drink.
options.rationale: Caffeine, energy drinks, and other stimulants are on the manual's list of methods that do not prevent drowsy driving. A wired brain is still a sleep-deprived brain.

options.text: Finding a safe place to stop and sleeping for 10 to 20 minutes.
options.rationale: Correct. The manual says a nap that short makes a real difference. Sleep is the only thing that treats the actual problem, which is a lack of sleep.

options.text: Chewing gum to stay sharp.
options.rationale: Gum is another item the manual specifically says is not a reliable way to stay awake. A moving jaw is not rest.

explanation: The Driver's Manual (Section 3, Drowsy Driving, p. 24-25) treats drowsy driving as a form of impaired driving. The signs it describes include yawning, heavy eyelids, head nodding, missing signs or exits, drifting from the lane, and not remembering the last stretch of road. Once those show up, the manual's fix is rest: stop somewhere safe and nap for 10 to 20 minutes, or hand the wheel to a rested companion. It explicitly rejects the folk remedies of opening a window, chewing gum, turning up the radio, and drinking caffeine or energy drinks. Prevention starts before the trip: get proper sleep, skip alcohol and heavy meals, stop at least every two hours, and avoid driving between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, Drowsy Driving, p. 24-25

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, p. 24-25

accuracy.note: Manual p. 24: warning signs list; p. 25: nap of as little as 10 to 20 minutes makes a big difference; stop at least every two hours; avoid driving 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; rolling down a window, chewing gum, turning up the radio, caffeine, energy drinks, and other stimulants do not prevent drowsy driving. No statute covers drowsy driving specifically.

stem: DMV receives a report that a licensed driver has a health condition, such as a seizure disorder, that may make driving unsafe. What can DMV do about it?

options.text: Nothing until the driver is convicted of a traffic offense.
options.rationale: The Medical Review Program acts on reports of a possible impairment, not on convictions. Va. Code § 46.2-322 lets DMV act when it has good cause to believe a driver is impaired, with 15 days' written notice.

options.text: Require a medical or vision report from the driver's doctor, or a fresh knowledge or road test, then suspend, restrict, or monitor the license as the results warrant.
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual describes exactly that process, and § 46.2-322 gives DMV the authority to require an examination and then to suspend, keep, or restrict the license.

options.text: Cancel the license permanently with no way to get it back.
options.rationale: Outcomes range from closing the review with no action, to periodic reports, to restrictions, to suspension. A medical suspension is lifted once DMV is satisfied the condition is under control.

options.text: Only a court can restrict a license for a medical reason.
options.rationale: Medical review is an administrative process run by DMV. No court is involved unless the driver appeals.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 46.2-322, when DMV has good cause to believe a driver is impaired and unable to drive safely, it may, after at least 15 days' written notice, require the driver to submit to an examination, and after that it may suspend the license, let the driver keep it, or issue it with restrictions. The Driver's Manual (Section 5, Medical Review Program, p. 29) explains what DMV looks at: any condition affecting level of consciousness, perception (vision), judgment, or motor skills. DMV may ask for a physician's medical or vision report and may require the two-part knowledge exam or the road skills test. Chronic conditions like epilepsy, diabetes, or sleep disorders do not automatically end a driving career, but they can put a driver into this review, and a driver whose condition changes should expect it.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 5, Medical Review Program, p. 29

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 5, p. 29

accuracy.note: § 46.2-322(A): with good cause to believe a driver is impaired and unable to drive safely, after written notice of at least 15 days, DMV may require an examination of fitness to drive; (B): DMV may suspend, permit retention, or issue a license subject to § 46.2-329 restrictions. History ends 2024, c. 414. Manual p. 29: DMV concerned with level of consciousness, perception (vision), judgment, motor skills; may require a physician's medical or vision report and/or the two-part knowledge exam and/or road skills test; outcomes are suspend, restrict, periodic reports, or end review. The seizure-disorder example in the stem is illustrative; neither source names specific conditions. Option c's reinstatement claim rests on the manual's paragraph about reinstating after a medical-review suspension.

stem: Since July 1, 2026, Virginia has a law aimed squarely at drivers who go live on a social media app while the car is moving. What is the penalty for a first conviction?

options.text: A fine of up to $500
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-818.3(D) sets a fine of not more than $500 for a first offense, on top of anything else the driver is charged with.

options.text: A $125 fine
options.rationale: $125 is the first-offense fine for holding a handheld device under § 46.2-818.2, the older distracted-driving law. Live streaming has its own section with a higher cap.

options.text: A 30-day license suspension
options.rationale: That is what a second live-streaming conviction brings. A third or later one is 90 days. A first offense is a fine only.

options.text: A Class 1 misdemeanor with possible jail time
options.rationale: Section 46.2-818.3 sets a fine for a first offense and license suspensions after that. It does not create a jailable misdemeanor.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-818.3, added in 2026, makes it unlawful to start, take part in, or manipulate a device to interact with a live stream while driving a moving vehicle on a Virginia highway, and separately to manipulate a device to keep a live stream running. A first conviction carries a fine of up to $500; a second brings a 30-day license suspension and a third or later a 90-day suspension, with another fine of up to $500 possible if the driver was in a crash at the time. Two details matter: reporting an emergency or a crime is exempt, and a dashcam that records without transmitting is fine. The law is secondary enforcement, meaning an officer cannot stop a car for this alone, unlike the handheld-device rule in § 46.2-818.2, which is a primary offense.

accuracy.note: Read on LIS 2026-09-04. (B) initiate, participate in, or manipulate a device to interact with a live stream while driving a moving vehicle; (C) manipulate a device to enable or maintain a live stream; (D) first offense fine not more than $500; second 30-day suspension; third or subsequent 90-day; extra fine up to $500 if involved in an accident; (E) exempt for reporting an emergency or crime; (F) dashcams and fleet systems that do not transmit are excluded; (G) no officer shall stop a vehicle for this violation. History: 2026, c. 1047. The exact content of 2026 c. 518 (amending § 46.2-818.2) has not been read; this item cites § 46.2-818.2 only for its $125 figure, which is current.

stem: You are about to drive to a friend's house you have never been to. Following the Driver's Manual's advice on avoiding distraction, when should you type the address into your navigation app?

options.text: Before you pull out, at the same time you set the music and climate controls.
options.rationale: Correct. The manual's first precaution is to set up the vehicle's controls and any devices before the car starts moving, and if something comes up mid-trip, to pull over and stop somewhere safe first.

options.text: While driving, as long as you keep each glance to a couple of seconds.
options.rationale: Those couple of seconds are the whole problem: the manual explains that a distracted car can drift into a hazard and the driver loses the time needed to react. Typing into a phone you are holding also violates § 46.2-818.2.

options.text: Once you reach a quiet street with hardly any traffic.
options.rationale: Quiet streets still have driveways, pedestrians, and cross traffic. The manual's rule is to stop in a safe place before doing anything distracting, not to pick an easier road for it.

options.text: After you are on the highway, where the road runs straight.
options.rationale: At highway speed each second with your eyes down covers far more road, so the cost of a distraction goes up, not down.

explanation: The Driver's Manual (Section 3, Distracted Driving, p. 24) lists three precautions: keep your eyes on the road and hands on the wheel the whole time, set or adjust the vehicle's controls and other devices when you get in and before you start driving, and do not use a cell phone. Its general rule for anything distracting that comes up later is to pull over and stop in a safe spot first. Navigation is a legal use of a phone under Va. Code § 46.2-818.2 only while the driver is not holding it or entering information, so punching in an address while moving is both a distraction and a ticket.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, Distracted Driving, p. 24

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39), April 2026, Section 3, p. 24

accuracy.note: Manual p. 24: distractions named include changing music/podcast/GPS, passengers, outside surroundings, eating, phones; before engaging in distracting behavior, pull over and stop in a safe location; a phone may be used for navigation as long as the driver is not entering information or holding it; precautions: eyes on road and hands on wheel, set controls and devices before driving, do not use a cell phone. The § 46.2-818.2 point in option b and the explanation is the handheld rule already verified in the bank (de13a-handheld-hold).

stem: It is a clear evening in July. The sun dipped below the horizon a few minutes ago, but there is still plenty of light and you can see the road without any trouble. Under Virginia law, when do your headlights have to be switched on?

options.text: Only once it is fully dark and you genuinely cannot see without them
options.rationale: The law is keyed to the clock, not to how dark it feels to you. Headlights at dusk are mostly about other people seeing your car, which is why the statute starts the requirement at sunset rather than at full darkness.

options.text: From sunset until sunrise, starting now
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-1030 requires lighted headlights on every vehicle operating on a highway from sunset to sunrise, so the moment the sun is down the rule applies even if you can still see well.

options.text: Beginning half an hour after sunset and ending half an hour before sunrise
options.rationale: A number of other states write their rule with a thirty-minute cushion on each side. Virginia does not: § 46.2-1030 draws the line at sunset and sunrise themselves.

options.text: Only if visibility falls below 500 feet
options.rationale: The 500-foot test is a separate daytime trigger in the same section, for rain, fog, snow and similar conditions. It adds to the sunset rule; it does not replace it.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-1030 gives three situations in which your headlights must be lit: from sunset to sunrise; at any other time when weather or poor light keeps you from making out people or vehicles 500 feet away; and whenever your wipers are running because of fog, rain, sleet or snow. The first of these is the one that catches new drivers at dusk. Do not wait for darkness. As soon as the sun is down, the lights go on, because a gray car against a gray sky is hard for other drivers to pick out long before you have trouble seeing the road yourself.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Night Driving, p. 23

accuracy.note: Subsection A(i) reads 'from sunset to sunrise'; (ii) is the 500-foot reduced-visibility trigger; (iii) is the wiper trigger. Latest amendment 2025 c. 252. Subsection F makes the wiper clause secondary-enforcement only, but an officer may stop a vehicle showing no lighted headlights during the subsection A periods. Manual p. 23 repeats the sunset-to-sunrise rule.

stem: Tomorrow you are driving three hours across Virginia to visit a friend. Tonight you want to find out whether there are lane closures, crashes or construction along your route. Which service is the Commonwealth's own traveler-information source for that?

options.text: Call 911 and ask the dispatcher about the roads
options.rationale: 911 exists for emergencies. Tying up a dispatcher with a trip-planning question is a misuse of the line and will not get you route information anyway.

options.text: VDOT's 511 Virginia service, by phone, website or app
options.rationale: Correct. 511 is the Virginia Department of Transportation's traveler-information system, and the Driver's Manual points motorists to it for construction and road-condition information ahead of a trip.

options.text: The DMV customer service line
options.rationale: DMV handles licenses, registration and titles. It does not track live traffic or work zones; that is VDOT's job.

options.text: Your insurance company's roadside-assistance number
options.rationale: Roadside assistance helps after a breakdown. It does not publish closures or construction schedules for planning a trip.

explanation: Virginia's official source for what is happening on the road is 511, run by VDOT. You can dial 511 from a phone in Virginia, open 511.vdot.virginia.gov, or install the free 511 app to see work zones, incidents, congestion, traffic cameras and weather along a route. The Driver's Manual specifically recommends checking it before a trip for road conditions and construction. Doing this the night before means you can pick a different route or leave earlier instead of discovering a closed lane at highway speed, which is also when work-zone fines and orange-sign speed limits apply.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 2, Message Boards, p. 11

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 2, Message Boards, p. 11

accuracy.note: Manual p. 11 directs drivers to virginiadot.org, 511virginia.org or dialing 511 for road-condition and construction information in advance of a trip. VDOT's travel page confirms 511 is 'your key to knowing what is on the road before you go', online and via iOS/Android apps; 511virginia.org now redirects to 511.vdot.virginia.gov. The VDOT page states 'Last updated: May 29, 2026', which is the effective date used.

stem: You are giving your one-year-old cousin a ride in a rear-facing car seat. Under Virginia law, when may that seat be installed in the front passenger seat?

options.text: Whenever the child is under 2, because rear-facing seats are built for the front
options.rationale: Backwards. Rear-facing seats put the infant's head close to the dashboard, which is exactly where a passenger air bag deploys. The statute sends child restraints to the back seat for that reason.

options.text: Only if the vehicle has no back seat, and the passenger air bag is either absent or turned off
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-1095 requires child restraints in the back seat; the front is allowed only when there is no back seat and the passenger-side air bag is missing or deactivated.

options.text: Whenever an adult over 21 is at the wheel
options.rationale: The driver's age has nothing to do with it. The danger is the air bag striking the child, and that is the same no matter who is driving.

options.text: Never; a child restraint may not go in the front under any circumstances
options.rationale: Too strict. The law does carve out one exception, for vehicles such as two-seat pickups that have no back seat, provided the air bag is not a threat.

explanation: A front passenger air bag inflates in a fraction of a second with enough force to seriously injure or kill a small child, and a rear-facing seat places the baby's head right in its path. So Va. Code § 46.2-1095 says child restraint devices go in the back seat. The single exception is a vehicle with no back seat at all; then the restraint may ride in front only if the vehicle has no passenger-side air bag or that air bag has been switched off. The Driver's Manual gives the same rule. Air bags were designed around adult bodies, which is why the safest practice for children generally is the back seat.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 4, Child Safety Seats, p. 27

accuracy.note: § 46.2-1095(A): 'child restraint devices shall be placed in the back seat of a vehicle. In the event the vehicle does not have a back seat, the child restraint device may be placed in the front passenger seat only if the vehicle is either not equipped with a passenger side airbag or the passenger side airbag has been deactivated.' Both conditions (no back seat AND air bag absent/off) are required. Latest amendment 2019 cc. 196, 319. Manual p. 27 states the same rule for rear-facing seats.

stem: You drive the same road home every day. Today it has been raining for an hour and the surface is soaked. Compared with the dry road, about how much farther should you expect the car to travel once you press the brake?

options.text: About the same; modern tires grip wet pavement nearly as well as dry
options.rationale: Tread channels water away, but a film of water still cuts the friction between rubber and road. Braking on a wet surface takes noticeably longer no matter how new the tires are.

options.text: Roughly 10 percent farther
options.rationale: That badly understates it. A small margin like this is what drivers assume when they follow at their dry-road distance in rain, and it is why rear-end crashes climb when the weather turns.

options.text: Up to about twice as far
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual gives wet pavement as an example of a condition that can double your braking distance, which is why it tells you to double your following distance in bad weather.

options.text: About ten times as far
options.rationale: An exaggeration. If rain multiplied stopping distance tenfold, ordinary driving in wet weather would be impossible. The figure the manual uses is a doubling.

explanation: Braking distance is the ground your car covers after your foot is on the pedal, and it depends on speed, brake and tire condition, and the surface. On wet pavement the water between tire and road lowers grip enough that the Driver's Manual warns your braking distance can double. That is the reason behind two habits it teaches for reduced-traction conditions: slow down first, and open up your following distance to twice the usual gap so the extra stopping room is already there before you need it.

source.citation: Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Stopping Distance, p. 15

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Stopping Distance, p. 15
Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Hazardous Conditions, p. 23

accuracy.note: Manual p. 15: braking distance is affected by speed, brake and tire condition and pavement, 'for example, wet pavement can double your braking distance.' Manual p. 23: in hazardous conditions, reduce speed and double your normal following distance. The 'double' figure is a manual example, not a statutory number.

stem: You are on a rural highway at 55 mph when a deer walks onto the road ahead. Virginia's official stopping-distance table allows an alert driver 1.5 seconds to notice the hazard and get a foot onto the brake. Roughly how far does your car travel during that 1.5 seconds, before any braking happens?

options.text: About 55 feet
options.rationale: This guess treats miles per hour as if it were feet per second. At 55 mph the car is actually covering about 81 feet every second, so 1.5 seconds is much more than 55 feet.

options.text: About 121 feet
options.rationale: Correct. The table in Va. Code § 46.2-880 lists 80.7 feet per second at 55 mph and a perception-reaction distance of 121 feet, which is 1.5 seconds of travel.

options.text: About 144 feet
options.rationale: 144 feet is the table's braking distance for a passenger car at 55 mph, the ground covered after the brakes bite. The question asks about the distance before braking starts.

options.text: About 265 feet
options.rationale: 265 feet is the total for a car at 55 mph: reaction distance plus braking distance. Only the first part, the reaction distance, is what the question asks for.

explanation: Stopping is not one event but two. First comes the time it takes you to see the problem, decide, and move your foot; the car keeps rolling at full speed the whole while. Only then does braking distance begin. Virginia's courts use the table in Va. Code § 46.2-880, which assumes 1.5 seconds of perception and reaction. At 55 mph that is 80.7 feet per second, so about 121 feet pass under the car before it even begins to slow, and a further 144 feet of braking on dry, level pavement brings the total to roughly 265 feet, close to the length of a football field. Anything that stretches your reaction time, such as fatigue, a phone, or a passenger, adds to that first number directly.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Stopping Distance, p. 15

accuracy.note: § 46.2-880 table row for 55 mph: 80.7 ft/s; perception-reaction distance 121 ft; automobile braking distance 144 ft; total 265 ft. The table assumes a 1.5-second reaction time and a vehicle in good condition on level, dry highway. Latest amendment 2003 c. 277. The manual's stopping-distance section cites this section as its source.

stem: Your car is equipped with antilock brakes. The car in front of you stops without warning and you must brake as hard as you can. What should you do with the brake pedal?

options.text: Pump it rapidly so the wheels do not lock
options.rationale: Pumping is the old technique for cars without ABS. With antilock brakes the system already releases and reapplies pressure many times a second; every time you lift your foot you switch that off and lengthen the stop.

options.text: Press it hard and hold steady pressure while steering where you want the car to go
options.rationale: Correct. The Driver's Manual's one firm instruction on ABS is never to pump it. Keep the pressure on, expect the pedal to pulse, and steer around the hazard if there is room.

options.text: Tap it lightly a few times to give the ABS a moment to engage
options.rationale: Light taps never bring the wheels near lock-up, which is the condition ABS responds to. You would simply be braking gently in a situation that calls for maximum braking.

options.text: Press the brake and the accelerator together so the tires keep turning
options.rationale: Driving the wheels against the brakes only fights the stop. ABS keeps the tires rolling on its own by modulating brake pressure; it needs no help from the accelerator.

explanation: Antilock brakes sense when a wheel is about to stop turning and momentarily release pressure on that wheel, then reapply it, many times per second. A rolling tire keeps its steering grip while a locked one just slides, so ABS lets you keep steering during a panic stop. To get that benefit you have to keep your foot down: press hard, hold it, and ignore the pulsing and buzzing you feel through the pedal, because that is the system working. The Virginia Driver's Manual tells drivers to read their owner's manual, practice before relying on it, and never pump antilock brakes. Pumping or tapping hands control back to the technique ABS was built to replace.

source.basis: Session 10, page 39; Virginia Driver's Manual, Section 3, Antilock Brakes, p. 15

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Antilock Brakes, p. 15

accuracy.note: Manual p. 15: if your vehicle has antilock brakes, understand how they work, check the owner's manual, practice, and 'never pump antilock brakes.' The firm-steady-pressure phrasing and the pulsing-pedal description are standard ABS operation consistent with the manual's instruction; the manual itself only states the never-pump rule.

stem: Your family's car, registered in Virginia, passed its state safety inspection last March and got a new windshield sticker. How often does that inspection have to be repeated?

options.text: Every six months
options.rationale: Twice a year is more often than Virginia requires. The safety inspection cycle in Va. Code § 46.2-1158 is measured in twelve-month periods.

options.text: At least once every twelve months
options.rationale: Correct. Va. Code § 46.2-1158 requires reinspection within twelve months of the month of the first inspection and at least once every twelve months after that.

options.text: Every two years
options.rationale: Two years is the cycle for the separate emissions inspection required in certain Northern Virginia and Richmond-area localities. The safety inspection is annual everywhere in the state.

options.text: Only when the car is sold to a new owner
options.rationale: Inspection is tied to the vehicle staying in use, not to a change of owner. A car that never changes hands still has to be inspected every year.

explanation: Virginia requires every registered motor vehicle to pass a safety inspection of its mechanism and equipment at an official inspection station, and Va. Code § 46.2-1158 sets the cycle: a reinspection within twelve months of the month of the first one, and at least once every twelve months from then on. The inspection, run under State Police regulations, checks the systems that fail quietly, including the service and parking brakes, steering and suspension, tires, headlamps, tail lamps and signals. The reason the state insists on a yearly look is that a brake pad wearing down to metal or a leaking brake line gives little warning to the driver until the pedal goes soft, and an annual check catches most of that before it becomes a crash. Any defect found must be corrected, and the Driver's Manual notes the vehicle must display a valid inspection sticker.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 7, Safety Inspections, p. 33

accuracy.note: § 46.2-1158: vehicles 'shall be reinspected within 12 months of the month of the first inspection and at least once every 12 months thereafter'; latest amendment 2020 cc. 1230, 1275. § 46.2-1157(A) requires submission for inspection 'of its mechanism and equipment' and correction of defects; latest amendment 2020 Sp. Sess. I cc. 45, 51 (effective 2021-03-01). § 46.2-1157 itself does not enumerate systems; the list in the explanation comes from the 19VAC30-70 section titles (service brakes, parking brakes, steering and suspension, tires, headlamps, rear lamps, signal devices). The chapter's most recent amendment on LIS is 19VAC30-70-80 (service brakes), Virginia Register Volume 40, Issue 10, eff. February 1, 2024; the other cited sections were last amended 2019-09-01 or 2020-09-04. Manual p. 33: annual safety inspection and a valid sticker required.

stem: You replaced the dead 12-volt battery in your car in the driveway. What does Virginia law require you to do with the old lead-acid battery?

options.text: Put it out with the household trash once it is fully drained
options.rationale: Placing a used lead-acid battery in ordinary municipal waste is exactly what Va. Code § 10.1-1425.1 forbids. Draining it changes nothing; the lead and acid are the problem, and each battery dumped this way is a separate violation.

options.text: Hand it to a battery retailer, or take it to an authorized collection or recycling facility
options.rationale: Correct. The statute allows disposal only by delivery to a retailer or wholesaler, a secondary lead smelter, or a collection or recycling facility authorized by Virginia or the EPA.

options.text: Bury it in the yard, since lead occurs naturally in soil
options.rationale: Land disposal is the thing the section's title prohibits. Lead and sulfuric acid leaching into soil and groundwater are the reason the law exists.

options.text: Keep it in the garage, because used batteries may not be given to a store
options.rationale: The opposite is true. Under Va. Code § 10.1-1425.2 a shop that sells you a new battery must take back at least as many used ones as you bought.

explanation: A car battery is a case full of lead plates and sulfuric acid, which is why Virginia treats it differently from ordinary garbage. Va. Code § 10.1-1425.1 makes it unlawful to place a used lead-acid battery in mixed municipal solid waste or to dispose of it in any way other than handing it to a battery retailer or wholesaler, a secondary lead smelter, or an authorized collection or recycling facility; a violation carries a fine of up to $50 per battery. The companion section, § 10.1-1425.2, obliges retailers to accept used batteries from customers, at least one for each new one sold, so the easiest legal route is to bring the old battery back to wherever you bought the replacement. Nearly all of the lead is recovered and reused in new batteries.

accuracy.note: § 10.1-1425.1(A) verbatim: unlawful 'to place a used lead acid battery in mixed municipal solid waste or to discard or otherwise dispose of a lead acid battery except by delivery to a battery retailer or wholesaler, or to a secondary lead smelter, or to a collection or recycling facility authorized under the laws of this Commonwealth or by the United States Environmental Protection Agency.' Penalty: fine of not more than fifty dollars, each battery a separate violation. § 10.1-1425.2 requires retailers to accept used batteries at the point of transfer in a quantity at least equal to the new batteries purchased. Both enacted 1990 c. 520, unamended.

stem: You are 17 and driving alone when you realize the map app on your phone is guiding you to the wrong address. What is the legal way to fix it in Virginia?

options.text: Type the new address quickly while holding the phone low, out of sight below the dashboard
options.rationale: The offense in Va. Code § 46.2-818.2 is holding a handheld device while driving a moving vehicle. Where you hold it makes no difference, and a first conviction costs $125.

options.text: Pull over and stop somewhere lawful, enter the address, then continue
options.rationale: Correct. A driver who is lawfully parked or stopped is expressly excepted from the hand-held ban, and the Driver's Manual says navigation devices are fine only when you are not holding them or entering information while driving.

options.text: Enter it with the phone in your hand, as long as you keep your speed under 25 mph
options.rationale: There is no low-speed exception. Any moving vehicle on a highway counts, whether in a school zone at 15 mph or on the interstate.

options.text: Leave the phone in its dashboard mount for the spoken directions, but pick it up to type the new address
options.rationale: Half right. Listening to directions from a mounted phone is allowed; picking the phone up to type is the violation, and it happens to be the moment your eyes leave the road longest.

explanation: Virginia's rule is about your hands, not about the app. Va. Code § 46.2-818.2 makes it unlawful to hold a handheld personal communications device while driving a moving motor vehicle on a highway, with a first offense fined $125, later offenses $250, and a mandatory $250 in a highway work zone. It does not matter whether you are texting, calling or fixing a destination. A phone in a mount giving spoken turn-by-turn directions is permitted, and the Driver's Manual says a device may be used for navigation as long as the driver is neither holding it nor entering information while driving. So set the destination before you pull out, and if it has to change on the way, stop somewhere legal first; the statute excepts a driver who is lawfully parked or stopped.

authority.cite: Virginia Driver's Manual (DMV 39, April 2026), Section 3, Distracted Driving, p. 24

accuracy.note: § 46.2-818.2(A): unlawful 'while driving a moving motor vehicle on the highways in the Commonwealth, to hold a handheld personal communications device.' (B) exception 2: 'An operator who is lawfully parked or stopped.' (C): first offense $125; second or subsequent $250; mandatory $250 in a highway work zone; driver improvement clinic possible in lieu of a first conviction. Latest amendment 2026 c. 518 (content of that amendment not confirmed; the statutory text as published is what is cited). Manual p. 24: a phone or telecommunications device may be used for navigation as long as the driver is not entering information or holding it while driving. The statute does not itself mention navigation. Whether a car stopped at a red light counts as 'lawfully stopped' is not addressed by the text; the item avoids keying on it.

stem: Your family lives in Fairfax County and registers its 2018 gasoline sedan there. Besides the yearly safety inspection, how often must that car pass an emissions inspection?

options.text: Every year, at the same visit as the safety inspection
options.rationale: This runs the two inspections together. The safety inspection is annual; the emissions inspection in the Northern Virginia program area is on a two-year cycle under Va. Code § 46.2-1177.

options.text: Every two years
options.rationale: Correct. The statute requires biennial emissions inspections for vehicles registered in the listed Northern Virginia localities, and DMV records the inspection as valid for two years.

options.text: Never; Virginia does not run an emissions inspection program
options.rationale: It does, though not statewide. Va. Code § 46.2-1178 names Arlington, Fairfax, Loudoun, Prince William and Stafford counties and the cities of Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas and Manassas Park, and a Richmond-area list as well.

options.text: Only once, when the car is first registered in Virginia
options.rationale: The inspection recurs for as long as the car is registered in a program locality. A one-time check would not serve the purpose, which is catching emissions equipment that degrades with age.

explanation: Emissions inspection exists to keep vehicles from polluting more than their emissions controls were designed to allow, and Virginia applies it where air quality is the concern: Va. Code § 46.2-1178 lists the Northern Virginia counties of Arlington, Fairfax, Loudoun, Prince William and Stafford and the cities of Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas and Manassas Park. In those localities § 46.2-1177 requires biennial inspections, so a passing result is good for two years and DMV will not renew the registration without a current one. Exemptions include motorcycles, a vehicle of the current model year or the three before it, gasoline vehicles more than 25 model years old, and vehicles running solely on clean fuels such as electricity. This is separate from the annual safety inspection, which applies statewide.

accuracy.note: § 46.2-1177: 'Such program shall require biennial inspections of motor vehicles at official emissions inspection stations'; excludes motorcycles, antique vehicles, and a vehicle 'manufactured for the current model year or any of the three immediately preceding model years'; latest amendment 2015 cc. 95, 161. § 46.2-1178(C): applies to vehicles of 10,000 lb or less registered or operated primarily in Arlington, Fairfax, Loudoun, Prince William and Stafford counties and the cities of Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas and Manassas Park; (B) is the Richmond-area program; latest amendment 2013 c. 634. DMV page: 'Inspections are valid for two years'; exempts motorcycles, gasoline vehicles with a model year more than 25 years old, vehicles over 10,000 lb GVWR, vehicles powered exclusively by clean fuel including electricity, and new vehicles titled for the first time for 4 years. DMV page shows only a 2026 copyright and no update date, so its effective date is set to § 46.2-1178's latest amendment (2013 c. 634, eff. 2013-07-01), the rule the page restates. The 2018 sedan in the stem is well outside the new-vehicle exemption in 2026.

stem: Maya, 17, is driving along Route 7 when her phone buzzes in the cup holder. She picks it up and turns it over to see who is calling, without unlocking it or typing anything. Has she violated Va. Code § 46.2-818.2?

options.text: No. Checking a locked screen is not reading or sending a message, so the law does not apply.
options.rationale: That is the shape of the older, narrower texting rule. Since 2021 the offense is having the phone in your hand at all, whatever you do with it.

options.text: Yes. Having the phone in her hand while she drives is itself the offense.
options.rationale: Correct. The statute bans holding a handheld personal communications device while driving on a highway; what she does with it once it is in her hand is beside the point.

options.text: No, provided she is traveling below the posted speed limit.
options.rationale: Speed has nothing to do with it. The statute sets no speed at which holding a phone becomes legal or illegal.

options.text: Only if she uses it for something other than a map.
options.rationale: There is no map or navigation exception for a phone in the hand. Hands-free and mounted use is what the law leaves open.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 46.2-818.2 a driver on a Virginia highway may not hold a handheld personal communications device — picking it up is the violation, not texting. A first offense costs $125, a second or later one $250, and in a highway work zone the fine is a flat $250. Think of it as a hands-off rule rather than a texting rule.

accuracy.note: Enacted 2020 cc. 250, 543; work-zone fine added 2023 cc. 557, 558.

stem: Jordan is 16 and his sister is 30. Because he is under 18, a police officer can stop Jordan for phone use under a special teen-only cell phone rule that does not apply to her.

options.text: True
options.rationale: The teen-only rule you may be thinking of was Va. Code § 46.2-1078.1, a total cell phone ban for drivers under 18. It was repealed at the start of 2021 and no longer exists.

options.text: False
options.rationale: Correct. There is no separate teen rule any more. One statute, § 46.2-818.2, applies to Jordan and his sister alike — and an officer can stop either of them for it, because it is a primary offense for every driver.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-1078.1, which once banned all cell phone use by drivers under 18, was repealed effective January 1, 2021 by the same act that created the general handheld ban in § 46.2-818.2. The current rule is the same at every age and is a primary offense for everyone, so an officer may pull a vehicle over for it with no other reason.

stem: Heading south on I-81 near Roanoke, you spot a minivan stopped on the right shoulder with its hazard flashers blinking. No police or tow truck is there. Does Virginia's Move Over law apply to you?

options.text: Yes. Any vehicle stopped on the shoulder, for any reason, triggers the duty.
options.rationale: Too broad. The statute names particular signals — flashers, caution signs, or lit flares — rather than the bare fact of being stopped.

options.text: Yes. A stopped vehicle showing hazard flashers, caution signs, or lit flares triggers the duty.
options.rationale: Correct. Since July 2023, subsection B of § 46.2-861.1 covers ordinary vehicles displaying any of those warnings, not just emergency responders.

options.text: No. The law covers only police, fire, and rescue vehicles with their lights on.
options.rationale: That was the scope before the 2023 amendment. It has since been widened to reach ordinary vehicles.

options.text: No. The law covers emergency vehicles and tow trucks, but not private cars.
options.rationale: Still the old boundary. The 2023 change added any stationary vehicle showing the listed warnings, a family minivan included.

explanation: Va. Code § 46.2-861.1(B), in force since July 1, 2023, extends the Move Over duty to any stationary vehicle that has its hazard warning flashers on, caution signs out, or lit flares or torches beside it. On a highway with at least four lanes you move into a lane away from the stopped vehicle when you safely can; if that is not reasonable, you slow to a safe speed and pass with care.

accuracy.note: Amended by 2023 cc. 616, 617. The former Move Over section, § 46.2-921.1, was repealed by Acts 2019 c. 850 — citations to it are dead.

stem: A state trooper has a car pulled over on the shoulder of I-95, blue lights flashing. The driver in the lane beside them neither moves left nor slows down. What offense has that driver committed?

options.text: A traffic infraction
options.rationale: That is how the ordinary-vehicle branch added in 2023 is graded. Ignoring a vehicle with emergency lights is treated more seriously.

options.text: A Class 1 misdemeanor
options.rationale: The statute does not use that label for this offense.

options.text: Reckless driving
options.rationale: Correct. Failing to move over or slow for a stopped vehicle showing emergency lights is reckless driving under § 46.2-861.1(A).

options.text: A civil penalty with no demerit points
options.rationale: Reckless driving is a criminal offense carrying six demerit points, not a points-free civil fine.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 46.2-861.1(A), not moving over or slowing for a stationary vehicle with flashing blue, red, or amber emergency lights is reckless driving. The 2023 subsection (B) for ordinary vehicles with hazard flashers, caution signs, or flares is only a traffic infraction. Subsection C adds a possible license suspension: up to a year if property is damaged, up to two years if someone is hurt or killed.

stem: Chris, 19, is stopped on the way home from a party and a breath test reads 0.03%. Virginia's under-21 alcohol statute covers which range of blood alcohol concentration?

options.text: Any measurable alcohol at all
options.rationale: The nickname suggests that, but the statute itself sets a real floor of 0.02%.

options.text: 0.01% up to, but not including, 0.08%
options.rationale: The bottom of the range is 0.02%, not 0.01%.

options.text: 0.02% up to, but not including, 0.08%
options.rationale: Correct. Chris's 0.03% sits inside this band.

options.text: 0.02% up to, but not including, 0.05%
options.rationale: The top of the range is 0.08%, where the ordinary DUI offense begins.

explanation: Va. Code § 18.2-266.1 applies to a driver under 21 whose BAC is at least 0.02% but under 0.08%. It is a Class 1 misdemeanor with a one-year license suspension and either a minimum $500 fine or 50 hours of community service. From 0.08% upward, the general DUI law in § 18.2-266 takes over regardless of age.

accuracy.note: Rule stable 2021-2026; amended 2026 c. 1112 without changing the BAC range.

stem: A 35-year-old driver's breath test comes back at exactly 0.08. Under Va. Code § 18.2-266, is that reading by itself enough for a DUI conviction, with no evidence that the driving was affected?

options.text: No. The per se level is 0.10, so 0.08 needs proof of impairment.
options.rationale: Virginia lowered its per se level from 0.10 to 0.08 in July 1994 (1994 cc. 359, 363). It has been 0.08 for three decades.

options.text: No. The reading has to be above 0.08, and exactly 0.08 falls short.
options.rationale: This is the common misreading. The statute says 0.08 or more, so a reading of exactly 0.08 qualifies.

options.text: Yes, because the per se level is 0.05 and 0.08 is well past it.
options.rationale: 0.05 is a level at which alcohol's effects can be measured; it is not Virginia's per se limit.

options.text: Yes. A reading of 0.08 or higher is the per se level.
options.rationale: Correct. Exactly 0.08 is included — the wording is 'or more'.

explanation: Va. Code § 18.2-266 makes it DUI per se to drive with 0.08 grams or more of alcohol per 210 liters of breath (or per 100 milliliters of blood). Because the statute says 'or more', a reading of exactly 0.08 is enough on its own. Any course material that says you must 'exceed' 0.08 is wrong at that exact number; the safe phrasing is always '0.08 or more'.

stem: Dana, 22, has a clean record. Arrested on suspicion of DUI, she declines to take the breath test at the station. What does Virginia's implied-consent law say happens for this first refusal?

options.text: Nothing. Taking the test is voluntary.
options.rationale: Driving on a Virginia highway is treated as agreeing in advance to be tested after a DUI arrest, so declining has consequences.

options.text: A Class 1 misdemeanor and a three-year revocation.
options.rationale: That is the penalty for a second or later refusal within 10 years, not a first one.

options.text: A civil offense with a one-year license suspension.
options.rationale: Correct. A first refusal is not a crime, but it costs the license for a year.

options.text: A 90-day suspension and a required driver improvement clinic.
options.rationale: That pairing comes from the demerit-point system, not from refusing a test.

explanation: Under Va. Code § 18.2-268.2, anyone driving on a Virginia highway has agreed in advance to breath or blood testing if arrested for DUI. Section 18.2-268.3 then makes a first refusal a civil offense with a one-year license suspension. Refusing again within 10 years is a Class 1 misdemeanor and a three-year revocation.

stem: Four friends, all over 21, are riding down Route 29. A back-seat passenger lights a joint while the car is moving; the driver does not touch it. Under Va. Code § 4.1-1107, who has broken the law?
